speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 139, to amend the Criminal Code.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to provide three amendments to the Criminal Code. The first is to do away with the provision under which the minimum sentence for theft of an article from a post office is three years' imprisonment. We are taking out the minimum because it has been found by experience that in a great many cases it is difficult to get a conviction when the conviction would necessarily entail a minimum penalty of three years.
The second is to increase the maximum penalties provided for defrauding the government in sales to the government of miltary stores. The maximum penalty was two years imprisonment or a fine of $5,000. It is proposed to increase that maximum to three years and a maximum fine of $50,000. The third is to substitute the Superior Court of Quebec for the Court of King's Bench for the hearing of appeals from summary convictions. The Court of King's Bench is the court which hears criminal cases with a jury. The sittings

of that court in the rural districts are quite infrequent, sometimes more than a year elapsing between one sitting and the next, but the Court of King's Bench is presided over by the same judge who presides over the superior court, which is the high court of original jurisdiction. The amendment would substitute the superior court for the Court of King's Bench so that appeals from summary convictions would be more speedily disposed of. It has been found in some cases that when appeals were taken from summary convictions, the appeal was abandoned when the court sat many months after the appeal was entered. This amendment will be in the interests of the expeditious administration of justice, because appeals may be heard at the ordinary term of the high court in each rural district.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening I was discussing the mechanics of the organization which this bill proposes to set up. I was endeavouring to point out to the minister the importance of the organization in the welfare offices in communities which were recommended by the pensions committee some considerable time ago. I had emphasized the fact that while we may have an efficient organization in Ottawa, it is not in Ottawa that the returning service personnel are going to demobilize, but back in the home communities. The machinery for dealing with this matter through the welfare offices is in my opinion entirely inadequate. Across Canada to-day there is one such office in Prince Edward Island, one in Nova Scotia, one in New Brunswick; there are two in Quebec, four in Ontario, two in Saskatchewan, two in Alberta and1 two in British Columbia. The most important machinery at the time when demobilization takes place will be these welfare offices. Returning service personnel being discharged to-day and going back to their home communities know very little about the programme of rehabilitation which the government has set out on paper, and unless there are efficiently staffed offices in their local communities it will be quite a problem for them to find out what their rights are under the demobilization and rehabilitation regulations. In Nova Scotia, for example, as I have already pointed out on many occasions here, while the office has a very capable person in charge, it is completely inadequate for the routing of returning service personnel into vocational training or securing for them the employment preferences which exist under the regulations. That office is located in the city of Halifax, at the extreme western end of the province. The largest percentage of service personnel from that province will be returning I think to the other end of Nova Scotia. I have endeavoured to impress upon the minister on one or two occasions the difference between that end of Nova Scotia and most of the rest of Canada, in that there is a complete heavy industry set-up there. A man returning from the service with any kind of disability, even if it be only five or ten per cent, is completely unemployable; there is nothing for him-. Only this morning I received a protest from the Army and Navy Veterans of the town of Glace Bay, and I have had letter after letter from returning service personnel to the effect that when they seek employment and go to unemployment insurance and selective service offices they are routed into the regular channel of the unemployed, and unless they are physically capable of taking employment
underground or in a steel plant there are no openings for them. On many occasions I have referred to the necessity of the appointment of a welfare officer at the Sydney unemployment insurance office. The appointment has been vacant for the past two years. A year ago the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) assured me in this chamber that the appointment was to be made immediately, and I felt very happy at this announcement.

speechtext:
Yes, I certainly suggest that; because, as. I pointed out to the minister a moment ago, the plea that it is not possible to secure a suitable person in that area is not well founded. The person to whom I referred, who applied a year ago was, I know, qualified in every way, but he was never given the opportunity of an examination. If there is no local interference, something is wrong in Ottawa with the civil service commission, and it should be rectified and this machinery set up now. While only yesterday I stated that all these appointments should be made on the basis of merit and under the Civil Service Act,
Department of Veterans' Affairs

the civil service commission will have to see to it that there is no interference with the application of the act.
The most important function of the new Department of Veterans' Affairs is to be the organization of these welfare offices back in the communities. Service personnel now coming back from this war are not being interested in this vocational training programme, because there is no one to sell it to them ; there is no one back in their communities to whom they can go who can point out the advantages which they can obtain from it if they utilize it to prepare themselves for employment in the future. I think the minister should endeavour as far as possible to set up welfare offices in every section of the country, so that the official who has the first approach to the soldier in the field of employment shall have had sufficient training to enable him to sell this programme of rehabilitation with particular reference to vocational training. It is only in this way that the programme which the government has mapped out will be implemented.
I also emphasize the necessity of vocational training facilities. In the province from which I come there are no such facilities adequate to handle the post-war problem if we are going to be realistic about it. Almost the only facility in Nova Scotia is the technical college in Halifax, expanded very little beyond its peace time basis. There was a training centre located at New Glasgow connected with the Clark Ruse Aircraft plant, but since that plant has been closed the school, too, has ceased to operate. It should be immediately taken over by the Department of Veterans' Affairs and made available to returning service personnel of our province for vocational training purposes. When you approach the average ex-service man to-day and suggest that he take vocational training, the first question he puts to you is, "Well, I am paid about $14 a week; I am obliged to go to Moncton, to Montreal or some other distant place in order to take vocational training, and with the amount of money which I am paid it is not possible for me to maintain myself in some other province* during the process of vocational training." If there were an establishment in the centre of the province it is possible that more returning service personnel would take advantage of the vocational training.
The same consideration applies in the matter of routing men back to jobs. While under bill No. 5, which I hope will be administered by this new department-it is now, I believe, handled by the Department of Labour-a man has a right to the job he held prior to
[Mr. GUlis.l
his enlistment, if a man in our province is leaving the army to-day, it is because he is physically unfit, and that being so, he is also physically unfit for the job he had prior to enlistment, because, as I stated before, ours is a heavy industry section and there is no light work. When application is made to the selective service offices for employment, the selective service or unemployment insurance officials have no authority to implement the rehabilitation regulations as applicable to exservice men. One man came to me and told me that when he suggested that something might be done for him by way of lighter employment than shovelling coal underground, the selective service official in Glace Bay remarked to him, "Well, if you can turn that discharge certificate into a light job, that is the thing for you to do." That is not selling the programme of the government; and while you have a programme on paper, unless you also have the machinery to give effect to it there is absolutely no use in having it.
In the matter of hospitalization, pensions, et cetera, I am pleased" that the minister has taken the necessary steps down in my end of the country to establish a suboffice. I hope that is not just a hope also. I am hoping that in the near future the personnel will be selected and the machinery put into operation. But I want to leave this thought with the minister. In my opinion, across Canada today, hospital facilities provided by the Department of Veterans' Affairs will be totally inadequate to meet the post-war problems, and I suggest that an expansion of hospital facilities will be necessary. The second thought I want to leave with the minister is that we do not repeat the performances of the last twenty years in the staffing of pensions and national health hospitals, putting them under the guidance of part-time medical officers, where the medical officer strolls in at eleven o'clock in the morning. He has his tea and he is in a rush to get out, and he has a line-up on the bench for a couple of hours waiting for him, so that it sometimes takes two or three weeks before the medical officer can discuss the case of a patient who is waiting for him.
I think the job of the pensions and national health hospitals across the country is to make a complete examination of the patient, and it is the obligation and responsibility of the staff of the hospital, including the medical representatives, to see to it that the best treatment is provided and that every means at their disposal be utilized in order to get the man well and in a position to go out and take his place in the economy of the country. But that cannot be done with part-time rep-

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
resentatives. That was one of the evils of the hospital set-up, as I saw it, after the last war and in the period between the two wars. I know that at the present time with so many of our doctors out of the country that may not be possible. On the other hand, there may be many doctors under national defence who have not very much to do and could be utilized in these hospitals until such time as a regular organization is provided.

I am glad to hear it.
I have no intention of discussing all the ramifications of the rehabilitation programme at this time. I merely wish to stress the importance of the welfare organization as it applies to the whole demobilization period and to suggest to the minister not to pin too much faith on the voluntary committees that have been set up across the country We have had a good deal of experience with voluntary committees. They have nice honorary jobs and they get their names in the papers occasionally, but they have not the facilities to do the job which is necessary in guiding and routing ex-servicemen back to gainful employment after the war is over. In some sections of the country the voluntary committees do a good job with such machinery as they have to work with, but in Nova Scotia, to the best of my knowledge, these committees have not even made a start on getting into contact with industry and accepting the responsibility for guiding the service man back to gainful employment. The thing we have to do now in every section wherever possible is to have a competent man in an office preparing files, getting in contact with national defence, securing relevant data on every service man in the country who will be returning to that particular area, and selling the vocational training programme, advising them on their rights under the whole scheme. Unless that is done, I see a good many headaches in store for the personnel who may. be handling the national administration of the programme.

speechtext:
From the district which I represent over fifty thousand volunteers took part in the last war, and therefore I want to say something with reference to the new consolidated board to be appointed by the government to handle the problem of the returned soldiers of this war and to suggest a cure for a great many of the defects that have existed in the various pension acts since the last war.
At last, after twenty years, we are apparently taking a forward step in the way of a
national policy and a consolidated department to look after veterans' affairs, something long overdue. Between the two wars we had five or six separate departments handling the various phases of the work. I do not wish to offer any criticism of those who have to do with one of the most important offices of government, under the head of this particular department. They have done good work, but red tape and technical small decisions have defeated the purpose of the act.
One of the reasons why I came to Ottawa in the first place in 1921, after the close of the last war, was the fact that callous indifference had been exhibited by all the authorities towards those who had fought the battles of the country in many wars and thus had saved it. But it was the same in the South African war and in the Red River rebellion of 1885. The veterans who in 1885 marched across the territory of lake Superior in the rebellion of that year did not get what they should have been given, or anything since. The same is true of those who took part in the Fenian raid. Grants of land were no doubt given them, but the lands were so far from the scene that they were practically valueless.
I am glad to note that the discussion on this subject is non-partisan, and I hope it will continue on that level. No doubt a forward step has been taken on the basis of service, in that the onus of proof will rest on the government. Every soldier who went overseas should per se be entitled to qualify for a pension. No means test should be applied, and what is given should include full compensation for the services he has rendered so as to enable him to take care of his family and put them back where they were before the war started.
Many of the very same points that were dealt with yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) were brought up and discussed by myself in the debate that took place on soldiers' reestablishment and pensions when I first entered this house in a debate on June 21, 1922. Some nine or ten of the questions referred to yesterday, which are still unsolved in this country, and which have been raised in various applications that have been made with respect to proof of claim, callous indifference to soldier families, and so on, were brought up by me at that time. The work that has been done speaks for itself. We all know that but for the soldiers who are serving in this war we would have had the awful horrors of war perpetrated right on our own soil and we would not have been able to restore the country. Indeed, all the money that has been
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

spent on the soldiers is only pin money compared to the money spent on material things, the building of railways, public works and many other things of that description. In the great war these men went away voluntarily. A million men went voluntarily from the. dominions overseas and 130,000 died on the field of battle in the common cause and changed the whole history of the world.
While we have had a pension act, there have been many defects in it and proper treatment has not been given either the soldiers or their dependents. I wish to refer to one or two matters which are not covered here. First of all, the housing situation; what is to be done regarding housing for returned soldiers? In the city from which I come there are only -62 vacant houses, less than one per cent. I go around the city of Toronto; I visit the homes. I find soldiers and their families living in cellars that are not fit for human habitation, aceordiug to some of our local soldier authorities.
Let me mention one of the first things to be done by the government in conection with this veterans' department-and by the way, that is mysterious wording-veterans-to give to a department that will have to do with boys just out of high school. In the city from which I come, 896 boys who came from the secondary schools have been killed overseas. They are not veterans. Some of them had cadet training in the schools. In that connection may I say that the cadet services throughout the country have done magnificent work in the three branches. I suggest that the cadets in the high schools associated with the navy, the army and the air force be given a dollar a day, three days a week while they are training as cadets for this war.
I would rather see this department called the Soldiers' Aid Department than Department of Veterans' Affairs. When the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) was speaking yesterday he referred to an industry in my constituency, Lever Brothers, that great British company. They have put out a very fine red book. They see all the soldiers' off. They are willing to take them back at their old jobs and give them a better job. They send them parcels, cigarettes and supplies, and they do a great deal in looking after the women and children while the men are overseas. They have carried on most glorious work in that connection. The president of the company is Mr. Naim, a patriotic worker and great citizen. The hon. member for Vancouver North also visited' this industry. The president told me and yesterday the hon.

member also said, that they have some difficulty in connection with this work in getting a complete record of the soldiers' services, et cetera. It is true that they have their attestation papers, the unit to which they belong and all that kind of thing; but there is no record of the soldier during the time he is away from the industry. I have pleaded with the government for over twenty years to reorganize the records office from top to bottom. I have referred to this on many occasions.
In connection with the victory loans, income tax collections and other matters they have a proper record. The victory loan headquarters can tell within twenty-four hours after the closing of a day's campaign how much was subscribed by a particular village, town or city. Our records office is very largely a relic of the South African war. We have made, so far as I can see, no progress. We cannot tell how many soldiers enlisted from any particular municipality, town or city. Our industrial employers are not interested in many of the small details. They are not interested in primary matters, in finding out something about the work of the soldier while he is away. That was referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver North. I have in mind a young boy in Lever Brothers who wrapped soap and who was given a decoration at the front, and has risen to the rank of captain. On his return he should not have to go back to the job he had before he enlisted. His company want to use his services, perhaps, in an executive capacity, not at his old job, because with training he would go from the bottom to the top of any industry if he had a chance. They will give him a chance yet. The industries are not giving the protection that they should. In that connection I should like to refer to the various local boards, women's organizations, welfare boards and others who are doing so much for the soldiers in the different municipalities. They have helped every war effort. In addition to that, our clergy of every denomination in Canada have done magnificent work in this war.
So far as the $65 clothing allowance is concerned it is utterly ridiculous. I see some of the veterans coming back from the front going around in winter clothing, because they cannot afford to buy a proper suit of clothes. Some of these men have been overseas for over three and a half years. This is the seventy-fourth day of the session. Surely the government can come to some decision. If it is a matter of money, what does money amount to when compared with seeing that these young people, many of whom have

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
borne the heat and burden of the war and some of whom-those not yet home-will be over there the sixth Christmas next Christmas, are properly clothed when they do come home. I do not like to see them on the streets in the civilian clothes they are wearing; and it is a bad advertisement, and unjust and unfair for the country, the way those soldiers are also housed. I do hope that something will be done along that line.
Ever since the outbreak of the war I have had on the order paper a resolution relating to the protection and treatment of the returned soldiers as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should immediately consider the advisability and urgent necessity of adopting improved measures for the better protection of all soldiers who serve in His Majesty's forces, and more particularly-(a) that a system of life insurance on all soldiers be established, to include provision for their dependents, both during and after the war, and to include, for three years after the war, provision for their insurance against unemployment and want, and free hospitalization; (b) that a daily allowance be made for local car fare and for free fares on Canada's railways, under the Railway Act (R.S.C.);	(c) provision for a revision and
improvement in rates of pay, subsistence and other allowances of all ranks, especially privates and non-commissioned officers and removal of existing inequality between all ranks; (d) a high-cost-of-living bonus to be paid to all
dependents of soldiers, adjusted from time to time and to include better allowances for their children; (e) provision for a moratorium from foreclosures, eviction and certain other immunities from debt while absent on war duties, and for six months after the war, and more adequate and improved housing for themselves and their families at low cost; (f) a better and more adequate and quicker system of paying the dependents of those reported missing.
I also brought to the attention of the house, first, a national policy of soldiers' insurance the month this war broke out, and the need of a Sparkman act adapted to Canada's circumstances. I immediately sent copies of this United States act to the three ministers of the forces and the finance minister, and frequently dealt with it here. First, some of it was adopted in the last war insurance measure. After Pearl Harbor I still advocated it here, and others have also done so since. I was glad to see that at the last session of the Ontario legislature two bills were passed along this line, one providing financial protection for members of the armed forces and the other providing protection for life insurance policies of those members who are insured. I am glad to see that some progress has been made in that connection.
With regard to transportation, I shall read a return made to an order of the house, on my motion, in that connection, as follows:

Surely, if all this money has been made, more in one year than in the whole four and half years before the war, the railways can afford to give some measure of relief to the soldiers by way of cheaper fares and better transportation all along the line than they are now doing.
With regard to this bill, the proposed veterans' affairs act, I may say that we should adopt more human rights regarding this particular problem and that bonuses, subventions and subsidies should be given all along the line to soldiers and their dependents. I hope the Industrial Development bank will do
383S
Department of Veterans' Affairs

something in this connection. Civil aviation, if properly utilized, will become one of the most important agencies for providing employment. I doubt whether we are going to get the benefit we should from the policy of the government. With regard to jobs, I believe the soldiers' children should be put back in the position they were in before the war. Why should the soldiers' children be penalized because the father has enlisted and gone to the war? Why should there not be a provision in the rehabilitation programme which would give an opportunity to these young people, the children of soldiers, to go to the high schools and complete the courses that the soldier father intended for them before the war?
Three years ago a return was made to an order of the house in my name showing a survey of hospital accommodation in Canada. It showed that there was not enough hospital accommodation to provide for the condition of affairs that existed three years ago. What is to be done with the heavy casualties that are occurring in Italy and other theatres of war? In the city from which I come it is hard for a civilian to get into hospital. It is true that the present minister has made some start in acquiring the east general hospital, but there will be ten or twelve times the hospital accommodation needed in that city before many days pass. I do hope that some more active proceeding on Sunnybrook will be taken regarding matters such as these.
There are some other matters which are covered by the proposed act. For some twenty years a great many deserving people have not been able to get the help they required. I agree with the policy that in making appointments to this department those who have seen overseas service during this war should receive the preference. It is true that there are in the present department a great many experienced men of other wars who should not be set aside, but as far as possible these positions should be given to returned soldiers.
I wonder if I could have the attention of the minister for a moment; after all, this is not the banking and commerce committee, and dear knows it is nearly time that committee made a report. I can wait, if necessary, but after all we are discussing perhaps the most important problem this government has to face at the present time. I have a case here of a veteran who was a forty per cent disability after the last war. I saw perhaps 350 people at his funeral, veterans of the last war and post office employees. He had two sons, one seventeen who has enlisted in the navy already, and the other a younger boy

who has joined a cadet corps. His widow is very nearly helpless, but she will be turned out on the street unless something is done for her. Yet when a matter of this kind is referred to the department nothing but callous indifference is shown. I am not going to give the name, but this man's number was 348266. His policy number was 8888. I am going to send this letter to the minister for his attention. I am sorry to interrupt him; he is courteous, but I would like the minister to look into this case, because he has given every consideration to numerous matters I have referred to him.
Many matters may be dealt with in this debate. Most of them were referred to yesterday, so I need not detain the house very much longer. In passing, however, I should like to refer to the great difficulty being experienced in this country in regard to domestic help. Many of these mothers have to go out and work; others have young children at home, many of them are now with child, and they cannot get domestic help. I hope something may be done about this matter, and I propose to put a question or two on the order paper concerning it. Reference was made to this situation not long ago in Britain by Sir Edward Grigg, a great soldier who has done so much for the empire. In a recent letter to the Times he had learned from a doctor that during the previous fortnight he had attended three miscarriages-
- 'for which he could find no cause hut grave domestic over-strain. The mothers were young and strong. They and the children they lost were just victims of an anti-domestic mania under whose influence all-powerful officials are instructed to act as though mothers, homes and children were of no account to the nation by comparison with factories and canteens.
Many of those officials do their utmost to help; others are hostile to domestic claims. But whether they be sympathetic or not, the result is that mothers and their children, born and unborn, are going 'to the wall. If race suicide is to be a national policy, firing squads would be more merciful.
Many maternity and child welfare clinics with their voluntary helpers are also struggling against blind official indifference or discouragement. I gave a disgraceful example to the Minister of Health a short time ago. But the official sabotage of maternity goes on, more destructive than German bombs.
Then at page 375 of the National Review for last May, where reference is made to this letter, it is stated that this correspondence drew letters from many people, and the Review goes on to say:
There was a general consensus of opinion that "something ought to be done" to relieve the over-strained mothers. But what? Mr. Bevin has from time to time let it be known that he has it in mind to organize, at some future date, a vague corps of domestic helpers. This reminds

Department ol Veterans' Affairs
us of the little boy who pulled the wings off the flies and then, surprised that they could^ no longer fly, -tried to stick them on again. What Mr. Bevin and his brother socialists do not know is that it is easier to pull down a social structure than to rebuild it. They are slowly acquiring this information at the expense of the community-in this particular case the price is paid in the lives of young women and their children. There is a remedy for this almost desperate situation, and that -is to release from the factories and workshops the women who are finding that work too heavy for their strength . and who are therefore unsatisfactory workers, wasting their own and other people's time. A recent report on absenteeism in the war factories shows that there are a great many women who stay away from work they do not like. If they were released it would not be necessary to "direct them into domestic work," they would find it for themselves either in -their own families or in other people s. Once the strait-waistcoat into which women have been forced is relaxed the domestic situation will get better automatically. We may add that 'the women's services strain the health of all but the very robust, and that- it can be of no earthly good -to the country to keep young women in uniform when they are perpetually in hospital.
I believe that if an investigation were made here, as it was made in Britain, it would be found that many of the young women in the three services are in hospital or not able to carry on for a great many days during the year. The women's army services and organizations have done glorious work in this war; there is no doubt about that. They have released many men for the army, the navy and the air force, but I think this situation should be looked into by the department in view of the lack of domestic help for the families both of soldiers and civilians. I know the hospitals and rest homes throughout the country are suffering from this lack of help, and I think that situation should be remedied.
To make a long story short, the key to the whole problem lies in the choice of men to administer this department. We have had am example before us now for twenty-four years, and we hope things will be conducted differently in future. Now I believe a number of very fine returned men both on this side and the other side of the house, who have taken a great interest in this work, wish to speak on (his bill, so that I shall conclude my remarks.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support bill No. 83 and the principle of establishing a department of veterans' affairs. This bill is vital both to the people at home and to our men now fighting overseas. Some people suggest that perhaps we are talking too much about the post-war period and the problems of rehabilitation, but I suggest that now, when our men are in action, is the time we should make them believe that
we are sincerely trying to make sure that their wishes and desires, their hopes and aspirations will come true, and that we will not have a repetition of what happened after the last war. I have in my hand a book called "The Aftermath" by Right Hon. Winston S. Churchill, which I have read a number of times, particularly certain chapters. At page 16, dealing with the immediate post-war period and the men returning from the war, he said:
The boundless hopes that had cheered the soldiers and the peoples in their tribulations died swiftly away. The vision of a sunlit world redeemed by valour, where work would be less and its recompense more, where justice and freedom reigned together through centuries of unbroken peace-that vision which had flickered over the battlefields and beckoned from behind the German or Turkish -trenches, comforting the soldier's heart and fortifying his strength, was soon replaced by cold, grey reality.
And then later on:
A cruel disillusionment was at hand for all. All men, all women, all soldiers, all citizens were looking forward to some great expansion, and there lay before them nothing but a sharp contraction.
The same sort of vision that the men in the last war had while they were in the trenches in France and Turkey is being had to-day by the men overseas. They are all looking forward to something better. They want to be sure they will come back to a Canada where they will have jobs at good pay. They are not asking for too much. But they do look forward to a Canada that will not be the same as the Canada after the last war. There must be no contraction, as Mr. Churchill said was the case after the last war. While we can discuss the affairs of the veterans it must, be understood that they are connected with the whole project that we have in mind for Canada, a project that will lead to expansion instead of contraction.
This bill proposes the setting-up of a separate and strong department of veterans' affairs which shall be responsible for the care, treatment, vocational training, reemployment and reestablishment in civil life of the veterans of the armed forces and the care of their dependents now and after the war. With those principles I fully agree, but there is one proposal lacking, and that with regard to the men of the merchant navy. We hear glowing reports about their heroic deeds at sea under difficult conditions. Many of them have had their ships blown out from under them three or four times. These men should have the same guarantee given to them as is being given to the men in the armed forces. It is true that they come under some of the provisions
Department of Veterans' Affairs

of the Pension Act, but this is not sufficient. In his little book, "When the Boys Come Home," Mr. Senior says:
Since merchant seamen are engaged in a normal civil vocation-presumably the one of their choice-the question of rehabilitation into
civil life after the war does not arise as it does in the case of a member of the armed forces who has been taken away from his normal occupation.
That is not altogether true. Many of these men left trades to join the merchant marine believing that they were needed, believing that they were doing their patirotic duty to Canada. I do not believe it is fair to separate them as Mr. Senior has done. No doubt he means well, but at the same time it is not helping the men of the merchant marine.
We have three responsibilities to the men and women of the armed forces. First, we must realize that the wrar is not yet won, that hard battles are ahead and that weapons of war must be given to these men in greater and greater flow. Our second responsibility is to plan for the kind of Canada that these men hope to come back to. Third, we must set up that streamlined machinery which will guarantee civil reestablishment and jobs to the men and women returning home.
The bill now before us is a good contribution in that direction. However, in itself it is not sufficient. We must have the broadest approach to this problem facing the men and women of the armed forces because we owe them everything. In order to show the aspirations of the men in the armed forces I should like to read something of what has been proposed by the men themselves. After a lengthy discussion, a document known as the charter of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment was prepared. This charter, which was submitted to the Minister of National Defence while on tour in Italy, states:
1.	The Canadian government has a moral responsibility for the return of the fighting forces into civilian life, with jobs.
2.	Security and livelihood for every citizen should be assured by all means available, notably minimum wrage, health and hospital insurance, and national security measures along the lines of the Beveridge plan.
3.	A large standing army, navy and air force sufficient to meet Canada's international obligations for the maintenance of world peace should be established and the active army should be given preference there.
4.	Out of the existing overseas army a Canadian group for attachment to the allied military occupation army should be established on a voluntary basis but maintaining Canadian identity and officered by Canadian reinforcements to be drawn from trainees.
5.	Preparations to be made forthwith to let men waiting discharge begin trades and other training as soon as possible to obviate the necessity for purely parade square routine. Existing educational personnel and trades school staff could be used as a nucleus for this purpose.
IMr. Rose.]
None of us knows as well as these men exactly wdiat they want and what they expect to find in Canada once they. come back, and by all means those proposals should be considered most seriously.
There are still some shortcomings in our treatment of these men which should be overcome. In this connection I agree fully with a statement made by Mr. Walter S. Woods, associate ..deputy minister of pensions and national health, when speaking to the Winnipeg veterans' welfare committee on March 7. He said:
I don't think our democracy will survive another experience like the thirties. These men returning from overseas must get jobs. The man who has seen service should be given special recognition by employers.
The fulfilment of what is contained in those words of Mr. Woods is the responsibility of government and parliament, of industry and labour. All must collaborate and work together to see that it is possible to give these men a better Canada. Organized labour is collaborating with the men of the armed forces to a much greater extent, I would say, than in the last war. In the memorandum submitted on February 25, 1944, to the cabinet by the trades and labour congress there is a full section dealing with matters affecting the armed forces. They recommend better treatment, and they deal with the problem of clothing allowance and emphasize the fact that $65 is insufficient. The memorandum of the Canadian Congress of Labour submitted to the government on February 21, 1944, says this:
The congress recommends that demobilized members of the armed forces be continued on full pay and allowances until they can be gainfully employed, and that the clothing allowance on demobilization be increased to at least $125.
Recently at a conference held in the city of Vancouver, organized labour, together with representatives from the legion, considered the problems of the returning men, the problems of the armed forces and the problems of labour, because they realize that you cannot separate one from the other.. They considered a master plan that would provide employment for the workers and for the returning men.
I want to refer especially to parents in connection with the problem of dependents and pension allowances. Since I have been in the house I have received letters from parents whose sons have been killed overseas, and in all cases the parents have been unable to get any pension whatsoever. There is one case which I particularly want to mention. Here is a man, the father of twelve minor children. His boy overseas, an air gunner, was killed. The father is blind in one eye,

Department of Veterans' Affairs
and has rheumatism, but he cannot get anything at all, despite the fact that it is recognized that the boy had supported the family to quite a substantial amount before he went into the forces. He sent S40 a month home to his parents, and now the family cannot get a single penny. Surely it should be possible, by an amendment to the pension act, to provide for helping the family in cases such as this. The father may earn $25 a week, but how does that help a man with twelve minor children?

I shall gladly do so.
Then there is the problem which has been mentioned by everybody, that of the clothing allowance. Organizations and individuals have all agreed that there should be an increase in the clothing allowance up to $125. I for one find it very hard to understand why $35 was ever fixed upon in the first place. It is true that it has been increased to $65, which is a step in the right direction, but it is still insufficient. I think I cannot do better to show how the men and the parents of the men in the armed forces feel about the clothing allowance than by reading this letter which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of February 29, 1944. It is as follows:
As the mother of two boys at present in the battle of Italy, may I say one went overseas in 1940 when he was 21, the other in 1941, when he was 19. I wonder if our law makers realize that many boys like ours went overseas at the youthful age of 19, 20 or 21, still growing, and thm clothing they laid aside to don their country's uniform will be outgrown, which means when they return to civilian life they will require a whole new wardrobe. How far, Mr. Law Maker, do you think the sum of $65 will go towards an overcoat, a dress-up suit, an everyday or work suit, shoes, shirts, etc., etc.,? It would not much more than buy an overcoat or one suit much less all the other articles they require.
It is a disgrace to Canada to suggest giving these boys anything less than $200.
A number of organizations as well as individuals have asked that the clothing allowance be increased to $125. It would be good news to those now fighting overseas if the minister were to announce publicly that this question had been settled once for all and that the clothing allowance is to be $125 for all men honourably discharged from the armed forces.
I shall not take more time, Mr. Speaker. A number of other speakers have dealt with the problems of returning men, and there has been unanimity almost amongst all groups. All that we need now is action on the part of the government to make sure that our returning men will receive the finest of treatment, which is a debt we owe to them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say, at the outset, that I have had the opportunity to come into contact with the veterans of the last war and to- become acquainted with them-. I have had the privilege of working, with them since 1918, because they did me the honour of requesting me to become their legal adviser and I was pleased to accept. I deemed it my duty to help them in their distress and to give them my assistance during the depression that affected so many people. I have known a great many veterans, as well as their wives and children. I have seen on all too many occasions, the distress undergone by those men who had brought great credit on themselves from 1914 to 1918 and who, on their return home had certainly not received the help and the support to which they were entitled. I have all too often noticed, for instance, that because a veteran was in receipt of a small monthly pension, he was denied employment opportunities, preference being given to others. He was then left to shift for himself, and he was only getting $5, $10 or $15 a month from the department of pensions. That is why, after living among them, and witnessing their distress, I cannot but support any action that may be helpful to those who are veterans of the last war and to the men who are fighting in this war.
Evidently, the legislation now before the house deserves all our support because, as I said -a while ago, its purpose is to help the veterans and, in itself, it is a very good enactment. I want to add, however, that it is not sufficient, as everyone knows, to have excellent legislation-this statement is almost a truism-since the main thing consists in having the law suitably applied, and in all fairness which implies that there will be no discrimination.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, whatever legislation we plan or pass, I submit that we will not achieve our purpose unless this act is applied fairly. We all know that it is not
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

enough to admit the existence of certain evils, not enough to make laws allowing us to establish such facts and then pretend we are trying to improve conditions if, in truth, we do not apply the remedial measures needed to root out the anticipated evils. I would like to add that, knowing the veterans, as I said a while ago, I realize that what they ask is not so much a pension-they want no charity from the government, from individuals or from companies. Those people have their pride like other citizens, and they want the right to say like everyone that they are able to earn their living.
Obviously a wounded man, one who has lost a leg or an arm, cannot, in civilian life, render as efficient services as a physically fit man. On the other hand, it is a well-known fact that there are in our industrial plants and elsewhere all kinds of jobs which wounded or crippled war veterans could fill. Our dominion, provincial and municipal governments should pay special attention to the cases of wounded men who will return home after the war as well as those of the veterans of the last war who are still living. I am convinced that our governments could readily find, for a large number of them, jobs which would enable them to earn a decent living. Moreover, our industrialists, tradesmen, business firms and even private business men should realize the obligations that we will have to fulfill towards veterans after the war. If it is true-as has been so explicitly stated-that they have retained their possessions, that our system has stood the test, that companies and business men can continue their activities, thanks to those who have fought overseas for five years or more, and some of whom will return home wounded after enduring untold hardship, I claim that all these industrialists and business men should make it their duty to find easy work for all these crippled veterans, so they may honourable earn a living. I shall go even further and state that it is the duty of the government and the new minister who will be directing this department to organize a liaison service between the department, and the industrialists and business men of the country. Thus they would be in a position to locate all positions available to veterans, and when I use this expression I mean especially the crippled veterans. The minister should undertake a thorough investigation through the whole of Canada, in order to find work for all those who have given their blood to safeguard our industries, and to preserve the institutions we enjoy at the present time. The minister should, after this comprehensive investigation, invite these industrialists and business men to offer employment for the crippled veterans.

The same pitfalls that we had to avoid after the last war may well be met again at the end of the present armed conflict. We must avoid any method based on political patronage. I am unfortunately aware that politics have often played an important part when a veteran was in need of a job. Let us avoid such partiality this time and let us make sure that every veteran shall enjoy the full measure of consideration he deserves, no matter what may be his political affiliations.
This week, Mr. Speaker, w'e have voted quite a considerable sum in order to provide help for the united nations. We have voted much money for that purpose during the last two years. The soldiers who are now fighting know it. The veterans of this war will remember the gifts we are making to-day. The men who have fought for five years will, on their return to this country, remind us who are now sitting in this house, of what w7e have done during this war, the gifts we have made. Will they not have a right, to ask us to afford them a decent livelihood for themselves as well as for their wives and children? It is therefore imperative that we should now devise some plan for taking care of the large number of men who are now returning to this country and of the still larger number of those who will come back after the war.
(Text)
In closing, I assure the government that I shall always regard it as a duty to collaborate with any government to help the veterans; and I hope that when good suggestions are made, even by members of the opposition, the government will not put them aside for the simple reason that they come from hon. members belonging to opposition groups.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always contend that when a man makes a public statement he should have knowledge of his subject. I was greatly interested in the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair); he spoke as a soldier, and concern for the betterment of the conditions of our soldiers after the war was the thought uppermost in his mind. I did not hear the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), but 1 read part of it, and I wish to pay tribute to him for his tenacity in maintaining that the indebtedness still owbng by veterans of the last war to the soldier settlement board should be cancelled. I agree with the request which was presented the other day by a delegation from a western body of soldier settlers, that these men now be presented with free title to their lands. I say that, knowing full well

Department of Veterans' Affairs
that there are those who would not make a success of farming if you gave them another fifty years to pay for their land. But we cannot legislate for that sort of farmer. The great majority of these men, I believe, did the best they could under very difficult circumstances. Therefore I am pleased, if it is going to help any, to support the resolution which asked for the cancellation of soldier settlers' debts and the granting of free title to these returned men.
I want to speak in this debate from my experience as a farmer. I support the legislation which has been enacted and the proposals now under consideration for the rehabilitation of returned men who must resume civil life when the war is over. As a farmer I am interested in the Veterans' Land Act; I believe that it is a good measure if properly administered. I do not think I can do .better than to read some provisions of the act as contained in this little booklet called "Back to Civil Life". I quote:
The Veterans' Land Act, which is administered by a director under the Minister of Mines and Resources, gives a new meaning to the term land settlement in the rehabilitation of exservicemen. The main purpose of the act is to assist suitably qualified ex-servicemen to buy and own a farm to be operated on a full-time farming basis or to buy and own a rural or semi-rural home (small holding) with the main income earned from industrial or other employment in the community. To give practical effect to this purpose, the act provides:-three distinct types of establishment; that the state shall bear a substantial part of the cost of each establishment by means of a conditional grant; that each ex-serviceman assisted shall be qualified for the particular type of settlement; and that he shall pay down ten per cent of the cost of land and buildings at the time of his establishment.
For veterans who have practical experience in farm operation assistance is available to engage in farming as a full-time occupation. Encouragement will be given to sustain the "family farm" as a Canadian institution.
For veterans whose normal sphere in Canadian society is in industry or commerce or in the field of agricultural employment, provision is made for assistance to be established in a good home, with small acreage of land outside the high taxation areas. Mechanics, carpenters, masons, electricians, factory workers and white collar men may benefit. It is believed that seriously disabled veterans in receipt of substantial pensions may be especially interested in this type of semi-rural settlement.
And then there is an inducement to fishermen to follow along the same line. I quote:
Small holding (coupled with commercial fishing). For the veteran whose normal occupation is in the commercial fishing industry provision is made to assist him to purchase a comfortable home, a plot of ground and fishing equipment required for his occupation.
Let me now read the financial provisions:
The act provides a maximum of $6,000 to cover cost of land, improvements, live stock and
equipment, including fishing equipment. The maximum for land and improvement is $4,800; maximum for live stock and equipment or fishing equipment, is $1,200.
As to terms of sale to qualified veterans:
At the time he makes application to purchase, the ex-serviceman must deposit in cash ten per cent of the cost of land and improvements, namely, $480. He then signs a contract to repay only two-thirds of the cost of land and buildings, or $3,200 over a period of 25 years, with interest at 3J per cent amortized. The annual payment including principal and interest is $194.14. The entire $1,200 cost of stock and equipment, plus $1,120-the difference between the cost of land and buildings and what the veteran pays-is borne by the state. In this case the state conditional grant is $2,320 or 38 per cent of the total cost of the farm establishment.
It goes on to say that in order to take advantage of this assistance the position of the farmer must be maintained for at least ten years, and if you wish to sell or assign your property, you lose the benefits I have enumerated. Let me now read another short excerpt from these conditions:
The veteran may select his farm or small holding in any location in Canada but the farm must be such that in the opinion of the director of the act it offers reasonable opportunity for successful rehabilitation.
Here is another interesting provision I should like to read:
Provision is_ made for the granting of loans at 34 per cent interest rate to veterans who own farm land and may require funds to resume farming operations. Advances not exceeding 60 per cent of the value of the land, or a maximum of $3,200, may be made to pay off a mortgage, effect improvements, or buy live stock and equipment. If an advance for live stock and equipment only is desired, the total may not exceed $2,500, or fifty per cent of the value of the land.
I have been much interested in this phase of the rehabilitation programme. Owing to circumstances over which I have no control, I have never been able to offer a word in this house in regard to these projects. I am very glad to have this opportunity to support what I think is commendable in the government's actions. About two years ago, before the act was being considered, and anticipating that I might not be back in the house for some time, I presented a submission to the minister of pensions in which I outlined my ideas of a land settlement act. I pointed out in these submissions that farmers with experience should be the only ones allowed to come under this scheme. I pointed out that returned men should have the choice of location, and that it was desirable that they should select good land in good districts. I did not think there was need of going beyond the boundaries of our organized municipali-
Department of Veterans' Affairs

ties; I believed that there was plenty of land available for the settlement of these soldiers right in our organized districts, where they could have the benefit of good roads, schools, churches, and the advantage pf electricity, which goes with any properly constituted farm. I sent this submission to the minister, and he replied kindly by saying that I would find that some of the recommendations would be contained in the bill. I think perhaps that is so, although I am not taking any credit
I wish to deal with another phase of this important measure. Let me call attention to section 33 of the War Veterans' Land Act, which provides:
No person, firm, or corporation shall be entitled to charge or collect, as against or from any other person, firm or corporation any fee or commission or advance of price for services rendered in. the sale of any land made to the director whether for the finding or introducing of a buyer or otherwise.
That is contained in section 33 of the War Veterans' Land Act. Now let me read my submission in that regard, which I made to the minister:
In my opinion, whatever measure is devised it should be administered in cooperation with the provinces and the municipalities. Especially. I would say, the municipalities. Municipal officials could keep on file a list of the lands available for resettlement, location, price pel acre and other information required by the land inspectors. This information kept on file in the municipal office would tend to speed up transfers and guarantee a better deal for all concerned.
I added:
I am sure that you will agree with me that the legislation proposed should not be enacted as a relief for the mortgage holders, either corporate or private, but for the reestablishment of our returned men in happy homes after their release from army life.
That was my attitude at that time, and I still adhere to it.
I was interested in receiving a short time ago a notice from a real estate firm stating that a meeting had been held by the Canadian association of real estate boards in Niagara Falls and that a committee had been appointed to interview the government and that a resolution had been submitted. I shall read the resolution:
Be it therefore resolved, that the members of the Canadian association of real estate boards in session at Niagara Falls, Ontario, this fifth day of April, 1944, petition the Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada: that section 33 of the War Veterans' Land Act be amended by adding the words "save and except to a duly licensed real estate operator," thereby permitting real estate agents to deal for remuneration in all lands required in this connection.

It will be noted that this resolution emphasizes the words' "save and except." If this resolution were given effect to, that one body would have the sole right to buy this land for the soldier settlement board. That seems to me to be bordering on a monopoly. I do not think that any association should have the right to be the sole agents of any company. Especially am I against any action of this kind being taken by the government. Our returned men will be coming back after offering their all in our defence and in the defence of our homes and families. Here is an association asking for their pound of flesh in securing lands for their rehabilitation. I kpow that the government has not granted any rights to any real estate agent or association. I want to bring this forward to the minister and to the government and to tell them that I support them in the action they have taken, so far.
I hope that they will not weaken. I do not want to be taken as being antagonistic to any legitimate business. I believe the business of real estate dealers is legitimate and that there is a place for them in this country; but in this one particular where we are fighting for proper treatment of our returned men I do not believe that this association should get its finger in this particular pie.
Now I wish to deal with another phase of the land act which I mentioned a while ago, namely, small holdings. These small holdings would be secured adjacent to industrial centres. I believe the provision is an excellent one. I believe that the families will be all the better off in a semi-rural home and surroundings, but I am thinking of how it will affect returned men from western Canada who have volunteered and offered everything. As the house knows, in western Canada, and particularly in the prairie provinces, industries are conspicuous by their absence. We hear ' a good deal these days about the decentralization of industry. I think that it is long past due. If we are to have a balanced economy, both east and west and in our country as a whole, we must have industries in the prairie provinces. Very few industries are located there at the present time. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) has contended that thus far the industries of eastern Canada have not been fair to western Canada-and I hope I am not misquoting him. Along with many other hon. members I agree in that. We have had industries in western Canada but they were subsidiaries of the big industries in the east. They came out to further their own business. They established industries or assembly plants in different cities throughout western Canada when times were good. But when we had the depression period

Department of Veterans' Affairs
in the thirties, most of those industries-and I know whereof I speak, because this is exactly what happened in Portage la Prairie; I could enumerate several of them-closed down because business was not good and they went back to the parent company. Some of the employees who were raised in the west went back with them. We lost not only the industries themselves but part of our population. I think that government measures should be enacted which would compel, if not those parent industries which I mentioned, other industries, to establish themselves in the west. If that is done, if we have industries in our cities or larger or smaller towns where a returned man can get a job and have his family living in a semi-rural district, this provision dealing with small holdings will be all to the good. But if that is not done, farmers from western Canada who want to establish themselves in a rural home adjacent to an industrial centre will not be able to do so and they will go back east. I do not think that is good for Canada. I think it militates against the interests of the whole country.
I did not intend to take up much of the time of the house, but in conclusion may I say that no government policy can bring the desired result without the whole-hearted cooperation of the returned men themselves. I think that these men must have the will to win and the desire to work. I believe if they have these two requisites that we shall establish them in happy homes throughout Canada, with benefit to the whole country. I hope that these men will not come back and find their interests unprotected. As the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) said yesterday, a political promise is not going to satisfy these men who have offered their lives in our defence; they want these promises redeemed. After reading the different provisions in the Veterans' Land Act and the other measures which have been passed by the government, I feel confident that the government have the best intentions in the world and that our returned men are going to be established in the country to which they belong.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
I have always urged that all veterans' affairs should be handled under one department. I think it is fitting that while our thoughts and our prayers are very much for the welfare of our men and women now engaged in the invasion and liberation of overrun Europe, and. yes, of their dependents, we at home in this parliament should be giving consideration to bill No. 83, an act to create a Department of Veterans' Affairs.
First of all I should like to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) with respect to this measure. I should like also to concur in what was said by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) with respect to titles to the land of settlers under the old soldier settlement board. I think the great problem is going to be the matter of rehabilitation; and as has been stated on different occasions, I know of no better lift that could be given to the morale of the men who are now fighting than an assurance by the government that we are now planning on how properly to rehabilitate and reestablish them in civil life when they return.
The minister has pointed out that up to the present some 135,000 men have been discharged, while another minister has stated that so far only some 3,000 have taken vocational training. That is a very small percentage, and I think is proof of the fact that the allowances are not sufficient to enable these discharged men to take the training they would like to get. On several occasions I have pointed out that I thought the insurance principle should apply to those on active service anywhere. That should be our basic principle. I have said also that the pre-enlistment physical condition of a man or woman for all future purposes should be considered to be that obtaining at the time of acceptance by the armed services. That would make it much simpler for the officials of this board to carry on its administration. On several occasions I have asked that the widow of a soldier who received a pension of less than fifty per cent should be entitled to hospitalization and medical care on the same basis as the widow of a veteran receiving a war veteran's allowance. Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver North very ably pointed out the difficulty experienced by many young wives, with their little families, in getting along under somewhat harassing conditions while their men are away fighting for all the worth-while things we in this land enjoy. I believe a great deal of consideration is due these young women and their families.
There is also the matter of the $65 clothing allowance, which I think everyone will agree is not nearly sufficient to equip properly a man who is discharged after having seen service for several years. There is also the matter of the Sparkman Act. I believe Canada should have had similar legislation to protect the legal rights of the men serving in the armed forces. If that had been done it would have been much simpler to rehabilitate many of these men who are carrying on under many handicaps in the matter of life insurance and



Department of Veterans' Affairs
other obligations which they are not able to discharge with the remuneration they are receiving. I say that instead of leaving this matter of legal protection to the various provincial legislatures a measure should have been passed by this federal parliament, or it could have been handled under the War Measures Act.
Something has been said already about land settlement by veterans. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) quoted from the little green booklet dealing with that subject. I do not know whether or not he entirely agreed that the matter was sufficiently covered, but I was privileged to be a member of the committee which dealt with the Veterans' Land Settlement Act. It was a very interesting committee, and many worth-while recommendations were advanced. On one point I do agree with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie; that is, that commissions should not be paid to real estate men. I agree that these people have a rightful place in this country, but I have some recollections of personal experiences under the soldier settlement board following the last war, when, I am sorry to say, many of these soldiers were settled on submarginal land. I have tried to point out, as have many other hon. members of that committee, that every possible safeguard should be adopted so that we shall not make that same mistake again.
A little booklet entitled "Back to Civil Life" sets out the three types of establishments under the Veterans' Land Act. They are for the full-time farmer; for urban and^ other workers desiring small homes near their employment, and for commercial fishermen. Provision is made for a government grant of $2,320 on land and buildings costing $4,800 and stock and equipment costing $1,200, with loans to ex-service personnel owning farms and repayment over twenty-five years at 3i per cent. Briefly that sets out the three forms in which this land settlement may be carried on. I believe this is a very worth-while act, because I do not know of any occupation in which a man can better quiet his nerves and raise a young family than in farming, under proper conditions.
If I may be permitted I should like to refer to what I said in discussing the Veterans' Land Act on July 20, 1942, as reported at page 4386 of Hansard:
As has been stated, it was the purpose of the dominion government to provide a measure of financial assistance to veterans, upon their performance of the prescribed settlement conditions, in order to permit of their engaging in agricultural pursuits, either as a full-time occupation or as a part-time job coupled with some other employment.

May I say at the beginning that if it were not for the fact that I have some faith in the future, and a hope that agricultural parity will eventually be established in Canada, I would not have been able to support the bill even in principle. In the great nation to the south of us, the United States, there has been parity between agricultural and other products for a year now, and under the Washington wheat agreement of June 27, 1942, signed by the Argentine, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, the representatives of these nations have recognized the basis of a parity price for wheat which will return a fair remuneration to the producers as well as being fair to the consumer. On the basis of these agreements, and having regard to what has been done in the United States, I think we may hope that we are doing these settlers justice by establishing them on the land, because we hope that they will be able to carry on under parity prices, in the future at any rate. As I say, if it were not for that hope I for one could not have supported the bill.
This bill is distinctive. It is different from the soldier settlement act, both in name and in principle. It provides for the granting of a loan, and refers to ex-service men as veterans rather than settlers. In connection with section 5 of the act, I have felt some concern because in the early years, under the old act establishing the soldier ' settlement hoard, the municipal authorities had very many difficulties owing to tax arrears. I remember our western municipal union executive having to make trips to Ottawa on several occasions to have these difficulties ironed out. I am happy to say this was taken care of under section 5, which reads:
"5. The main purpose is to establish the legal entity and corporate powers of the director."
Then at page 4387 I said:
A great difficulty under the old soldier settlement board was that the authorities allowed these settlers to settle on a great amount of submarginal land. We cannot take too many precautions to prevent a repetition of settlement even in small numbers on submarginal lands, because it is detrimental both to the settler and to the country as a whole. We must guard against that at any cost. I should like to recommend that to avoid such difficulties our regional or provincial advisory committee should include a provincial soil expert from the university of that province, a representative of each provincial municipal organization of the province-because I do not know of any organization which would be more interested than the municipality in which the settler is placed- and a member of the provincial command of the Canadian Legion. Without their approval no settler should be settled on any land.
I believe the approval of a soil expert is most important, because the vast majority of the difficulties under the old settlement board came about as a result of the settlement of submarginal lands. In most provinces, certainly in the three prairie provinces, much has been accomplished during the past few years in connection with soil surveys by the experts of the provincial governments, and I believe any settlement under this

Department of Veterans' Affairs
scheme certainly should be guided by the findings of these surveys. It is all-important in connection with any land settlement scheme that these men should be placed upon the very best land available. In making his statement on this bill the minister said:
The Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment was responsible for many services in connection with the placement of discharged men in civil life with one definite exception, that of land settlement, which was placed under the Minister of the Interior. The measure to be based upon this resolution will place both the Veterans' Land Act and the other soldier settlement system under the Department of Veterans' Affairs. That was one of the recommendations hon. gentlemen will recall that was made to this house by the same select committee which studied the question of land settlement and which was responsible for the amendments to the Veterans' Land Act adopted by the house at that time.
I want to compliment the minister upon making a step in the right direction, upon doing something for which many of us have asked for many years. Let me repeat that I think it is all to the good that all veteran matters are included in the one department.
As has been pointed out in other arguments, probably the minister does not have his own way in these matters. It has been stated that the great difficulty in this matter, as in many others, rests with the treasury board. It has been pointed out that of the six members of the treasury board, only one is an ex-service man. It has been very difficult to get matters through the treasury board, but I trust that those people and the government will realize that they owe-I was going to say a debt of gratitude, but it is not a debt of gratitude- something which is due to the service man as a right, that they owe him proper rehabilitation and reestablishment after the war.
These service men made the worth-while things of life possible for us all. In many cases their wives and children have undergone hardship quite apart from having to put in many years without the guidance and assistance of the good husband and father. I know the government will be supported by the people of this country in the proper spending of money for the rehabilitation, reestablishment and general welfare of these people and their dependents.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) in speaking on this bill expressed satisfaction at the consolidation of various departments into one. He said he was heartily in favour of that and then he went on to say:
Nothing is more disheartening to persons seeking information or 'help from the government than to be passed from department to department to department.
100-242J
He said that now he would be able to go to this one department, go to one man so to speak, in order to deal with any soldier troubles. I heartily endorsed his belief in that expression. I, too, thought what a beautiful thing it would be to be able to go to just one man, whether you wished to take up the case of a soldier wanting to get out of the army, a soldier who wanted a pension, or a soldier who wanted to be buried. No matter what it was in connection with the returned man, it could be dealt with in one place. However, I am afraid the hon. member for Vancouver North is due for disillusionment as I was. That is not the picture as it now presents itself.
On May 30 I wrote to the department about a man's -case. Like many other cases, there were several things to be taken up. There was the question of pension, for one thing, as well as other matters. It had been stated that this man had been discharged as being unable to meet required military physical standards. This man had suffered considerably in Sicily, Algeria and Africa; he had been wounded and had contracted a serious disease. The man's wife or somebody thought that was a rather cold way to treat him, to discharge him as being unable to come up to the military requirements. There was some other stuff like that.
It was stated also that while in a mental hospital he had been asked to sign a discharge which contained as a condition the release of the government from all liability. That did not make sense to me. I do not believe that such things are true, but those were among the things I took up with the department. I got a letter back from the pension commission dealing with the pension angle and saying that they would try to get me replies to the questions which were outside the province of the pension commission. I got another letter a fortnight later which dealt with the pension case, but dismissed the rest of the matters with this language:
The other questions referred to in your letter are matters which come under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence.
So that I have to begin all over again the weary trail of discovering which of these gentlemen is the man to deal with, which is the man to put the matter before and have it pushed along. Some of them are not too ready to exert themselves too much to push matters along unless they are exactly down their own alleys. A couple of years ago I wrote to an official about a certain matter. I said, "Possibly this does not come immediately within your jurisdiction, but, if not, would you be kind enough to send it along to
Department of Veterans' Affairs
