speechtext:
I am always moderate in my language and I want to give the government the benefit of the doubt. The first time it is a mistake; the next time it is an accident, and the third time it is a habit. It has become a habit to pass a sort of skeleton bill which readily goes through the house because we are in a hurry to go home. When we ask about things we are told that they will be fixed up in the regulations. Then, when the regulations come down we find that substantially a new bill has been introduced. I am thinking, for instance, of the Old Age Pensions Act. By means of regulations they created practically a new bill, and that sort of thing is going on all the time.
By whom are the regulations made? They are made by the officials. We do not suppose

that the minister sits down and makes them because he has a lot of other things to do. Officials are apt to get into a rut. The way it works out is that these regulations contain perhaps the minister's ideas, perhaps the deputy minister's ideas and then the ideas of some of the officials. The great temptation is for the officials to draw up the regulations in such a way that they will be convenient to carry out. I have been a government official myself and I know my instinct was to stall off the man who wrote me the first letter.
There is another department-it is not the minister's-where they are definitely inclined to draw up regulations that will be convenient to carry out rather than to meet the interests of business or of the common people. There is no control over these regulations. Of course it will be said that I am quite wrong, that they have to be laid on the table within fifteen days after they are made if parliament is then sitting, and, if not, then within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session. But have we any control over that? Not at all. They are to be laid on the table. Last session we left here at the beginning of August and came back at the end of January, and any orders in council passed during that interval remained more or less unobtainable by us until we came back here in January. The section says that they shall be laid on the table within fifteen days if parliament is then sitting. We seem to be sitting a great portion of the time, and one might think we can get these orders in council. This "laid on the table" has a wonderful sound to our constituents. It sounds almost as if it were laid on our breakfast tables. But that is not at all what it means. It may mean nothing. The Minister of Pensions and National Health was kind enough yesterday, when he brought down his order in council, to lay it on the table and to give orders, quite without legal justification so far as I know, that it should be printed at once, and I got a copy of it a couple of hours ago. That was very fine. But ordinarily when an order in council is laid on the table it is sent down to Mr. Boulet's office and you can go down there and see it. Ordinarily only one copy of it is made, although in some cases there are two copies, and you can keep one of those copies for twenty-four hours. Then Mr. Bordet's staff telephones you and says that somebody else wants it. It is true that you can demand a copy, but there is only one solitary stenographer in that office and there are 245 members of the house, and if only half of them asked for a copy it would be a big order for one stenographer. Are we to put on extra staff for that?

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
The other day I asked for an order in council that had been passed. It consisted of forty typewritten foolscap pages, and I had not the audacity to ask that one girl to sit down and copy those forty pages, with perhaps Mr. Jones coming along the next minute and asking for another copy. I said to myself that this order in council must be available in a certain department and perhaps I can get a copy from the minister. I was told by an obliging secretary that I could, but he telephoned later and said he was sorry that only six copies had been made and I could not get one. Suppose half of us had wanted a copy of that forty-page order in council. Laying it on the table is more or less-I will not say it is a farce, but it is unworkable, so far as being available to the members.
The minister of pensions was kind enough to order this particular order in council printed, which he had no legal authority to do, and we have all got it. He has done a grand thing. The principle is sound. He has wiped out all orders in council which have been passed in days gone by and has made a new record. We can now study it and when an ex-soldier comes along we shall be able to discuss the section that refers to him. But it should be arranged, so to speak, that we can get copies of orders in council and get them readily. Even if we have the orders in council, perhaps we do not like the look of them. They have not been passed by this house and perhaps we may feel like kicking. Surely the government has some control. I say without hesitation that these regulations are more comprehensive and more difficult to handle than the bill itself. Is there any control? Oh, yes, there is control because the minister has to get them passed by council. That means the cabinet. I never was in the cabinet, but I have a vague idea that each member of the government has his own troubles and when he brings down regulations and places them before the council the others are not going to oppose his regulations for fear he might do the same to theirs. There is no parliamentary control.
Most of these things happening nowadays have happened before. I wTant to read a short paragraph from the London Daily Mail, which has the same credence perhaps as its namesake in Toronto, possibly more. The article is headed "Stop on Delegated Legislation", and reads:
The British government's acceptance of a check on delegated legislation will be welcomed by the country.
Delegated legislation is, of course, the system under which general laws are made-
Like this one here.
-and the details left to be filled in by the departments in the form of orders and regulations.
The new check is to take the form of a scrutinizing committee, which will examine every order and, if necessary, report on it to parliament. It will then be for members to take what action they think fit.
It would be wrong to regard this move as. a victory for legislature over the executive. Both, under the crown, form the government of the country.
We may look upon it as just one more example of how the British unwritten constitution, "broadening down from precedent to precedent," is elastic enough always to serve the needs of the times.
That is just where we fall down. We are too prone to statute legislation, to passing laws that do not work. We ought to have a scrutinizing committee applying not only to these regulations but to all regulations. I submit that to the minister and to the government. I am quite certain that it will not be accepted because they never do. It would be too much for them to yield to democracy as against bureaucracy.
There is another phase. Be the regulations good, bad or indifferent, there is one thing we ought to know about them, and know quickly. We ought to know what they are and when they come into effect. That we can achieve by an amendment to the bill. What publicity do they get? Subsection 2 of section 7 says:
All regulations made hereunder approved by the governor in council shall be laid before parliament within fifteen days after they are made if parliament is then sitting, and if not, then within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
The next ensuing session is a long time away, and if the house is not sitting the regulations are practically unobtainable. The only publicity apparently is to lay them on the table. I might put in a modest kick right here. I do not know if I should, because he is a good friend of mine, but I should like to know why the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) enjoys the privilege which I do not have of getting an advance copy of the regulations. He said on June 14 that the minister had been kind enough to send him a copy, "since the house began its session this afternoon". I have great respect for the hon. member's legal erudition and his ability to handle these matters, but for that very reason he is not entitled to any more privilege than I am in this matter because I have not his legal mind and so on, and people in the far corner of the house and myself are therefore entitled to get the information before him Why should he get it twenty-four hours before we get it?

Mr. Speaker, I believe this is the stage at which it is usual and customary to consider the fundamental principles involved in any bill under discussion. While I am concerned, of course, about the details of the bill, I wish at this time to occupy a few minutes in considering the fundamentals and the objectives which are involved in it. The explanatory note indicates that its object is the reestablishment in civil life of ex-members of the armed forces and of persons otherwise engaged in pursuits relating to the war, and for the care of the dependents of such persons. The object is the reestablishment in civil life of these various persons mentioned.
I have listened to all the speeches which have been made thus far, and I have been endeavouring to ascertain what, in the minds of hon. members who have spoken, constitutes reestablishment and upon what premise reestablishment is based. I think it is conceded by all that the success of any undertaking, whether it be on the part of a government or on the part of an individual, is dependent upon the soundness of the premise upon which the action is based. I should like to examine into the soundness of the premise that has been laid down or suggested by practically all hon. members who have thus far spoken. What is to be the means by which members of the armed forces, and those who have done their share in the war industries and in industries related to the war effort, are to be reestablished? What is the means suggested by hon. members thus far for reestablishment? I would say that in every case hon. members have implied and stated that the means to reestablishment is employment, jobs, full employment. Every member in turn who has thus far spoken has repeatedly stated that reestablishment of members of the armed forces and of others is dependent upon providing jobs and employment for them.
At this stage of our economic history and life it is imperative that we make absolutely sure we recognize, in contemplated action, a sound premise, and I wish to put the question to hon. members who have spoken, to the government, to the minister and to those who are still to speak: Is employment, jobs for all, full employment a sound premise upon which to base any proposal?
Department of Veterans' Affairs

First of all, before we can even intelligently discuss the subject we must have an understanding of what is involved in full employment. I would ask hon. members, when they say that we must have jobs for all, that we must have full employment, that we must have employment for everyone, exactly what do they mean by that term? All intelligent discussion commences with a definition of terms, and we shall make no progress in this house or anywhere else until we define our terms. I have put this question on previous occasions in this house, asking hon. members, when they discuss the question of full employment, to indicate what they have in mind with regard to that term, and I have not heard anyone so far define the term "full employment". We see the term used in newspaper editorials and articles published everywhere these days: "Our objective in the post-war world must, be full employment." But I have not yet seen anyone indicate what he understands by full employment. Do those who have suggested full employment as the objective mean that none of the people of Canada, the armed forces and those in civilian life, shall enjoy the standard of living they ought to enjoy at this stage in our economic history, unless they put in eight or ten or twelve hours of work a day? Is that what hon. members understand by the term "full employment"?
I should like to hear them indicate so.
Will they suggest that it is impossible for the people of Canada to enjoy a high standard of living unless they put in eight or ten or twelve hours a day? I should like to hear a commitment on the part of the minister, or of the government, or of hon. members, or of anyone else who discusses the subject, whether that is what they believe. We ought to know. It is imperative that we should know what they understand by that term. Or do those who suggest full employment as the means to reestablishment mean by that term that no one is entitled to live unless he puts in eight or ten or twelve hours a day? Is that what they ^understand by the term "full employment"? Or do hon. members understand by that term that the people of Canada shail not be obliged to do any more work than what the machines are unable to do? Or, to put it another way: Do hon. members believe that full employment means that the people of Canada shall be permitted to enjoy all the production of Canada up to the limit of their desire to consume? It is imperative that we have some discussion of that aspect because it is fundamental to the question under discussion at the moment and to all similar questions.
_ This question arises again and again. There is scarcely a department that is considered in

this house in reference to which the question does not come up. The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) said some excellent things yesterday, and he is well aware of that fact, for he said:
Therefore our entire programme of rehabilitation should be based on the assumption that adequate employment will be available. If that is not so, our programme of rehabilitation will be nothing but a programme of glorious relief, with a little training thrown in to pass the time away.
I do not think one needs to be a prophet to say that that is exactly what is going to happen. The present government had five years prior to the war in which to find jobs for all, and our friends the Conservatives had a term of five years in which to endeavour to find jobs for all, and they both failed miserably.

We did not have the problem of production prior to the outbreak of the war. There were goods on every hand and the shelves were filled up with them. There were ample supplies of every commodity. The problem we were faced with was one of distribution. That will be much more the case when the war is over. That is the problem to which both the government and the official opposition ought to be directing their atten-



Department oj Veterans' Affairs
tion. Thus far in this bill as well as in others the only means of distribution which has been suggested is employment of people. The term used is, "work-creating jobs". I am endeavouring to point out that the distribution of goods which will be available in Canada after the war can not be accomplished by providing employment; for in the first place I say it is impossible, and in the second place I say it is undesirable.
I wish to put one or two figures on the record, particularly for the benefit of the hon. member for Davenport and of all others who think like him, with regard to the situation that confronts us in industry. I have repeatedly made the statement that we are living at a stage in our economic history in which the power machine has displaced human labour to the point where the number of hours of work necessary to produce a high standard of living in Canada is far less than what is indicated by most people to-day. Most people to-day think in terms of working an eight-hour day. The fact of the matter is that the substitution of solar energy for human energy has taken place to such a point that the number of hours necessary to produce a high standard of living could be much less than eight hours a day.

Well, sir, I shall conclude that portion of my remarks simply by saying that I am heartily in accord with the objective of chis bill. No one could be otherwise. Those members of the armed forces who will be so fortunate as to return to Canada, one of the greatest countries in the world, certainly will be worthy of a way of life the like of which we have yet to see. But I must say with regret that I am convinced that neither this bill nor any other measure either on the order paper or on the statute books will provide mch a standard of living. I believe that we must raise our sights as to what constitutes a, genuine way of life far higher than anything we have done in the past. In years gone by our life has consisted of the somewhat sordid task of merely making a living; and I sincerely believe that the nation's heroes, as well as its civilians, should be permitted to enjoy life as an art. We must reorganize our whole national life so that our efforts will be directed to the art of living rather than to the mere making of a living. At this stage of our economic history it is not only possible for the people of Canada to enjoy a high standard of living as far as material things are concerned ; if we organize our national life properly it is physically possible for people to enjoy a good deal of leisure time, during which they may give expression to their creative instincts. That is an aspect of our national life which I am afraid has been greatly neglected. Through the laws which have remained on our statute books we have obliged our people to spend most of their time in merely thinking about the next meal. In the post-war world this country should provide a very high standard of living in material things with a much shorter work day, perhaps as low as four hours, with a per capita income much higher than it is at the present time. Certainly this country can provide in material things an income of well over $4,000 a year

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the bill which is before the house for consideration is evidently of great importance and, I think, meets with quite general approval by the members of the house, judging from the speeches already delivered. I have not had an opportunity of studying the bill in particular, having arrived only yesterday in the house, but I have read it over and from what I can see I believe it will meet not only with the general approval of hon. members but with the approval of the public.
As was said yesterday by one hon. member, the establishment of a Department of Veterans' Affairs is possibly long overdue. All the legislation in connection with veterans' affairs passed since the last war has met with change after change. It has been a sort of evolution. I am satisfied that this department will be one of the most difficult departments to administer. It will have to do with human affairs, and we all know that when you are dealing with such matters you run into more difficulty than when you are dealing with more abstract things. I think it is wise to have all possible plans made as soon as possible. On many occasions criticism has been offered in this house because of the lack of preparation after the last war. But we should remember that the last war came to a very sudden end in 1918; it ended much more quickly than was expected by the contestants or by the people generally. That may happen in this war, although that is something we can only hope for rather than expect.
I have heard it said at different times that the men in the armed forces are thinking keenly of what is to happen when the war is over. I have had considerable to do with the armed forces during the last four years, and personally I do not think I can state what these men are asking for or what they are thinking as far as the after-war period is concerned. But I do know that what is uppermost in the minds of the men of the forces at the
present time is the wunning of the war. That is their first consideration and great determination. Another matter which is giving them considerable thought is the question of reinforcements, or whether or not well-trained men will be available to give them sufficient backing in the great task which lies ahead of them.
The men in the armed forces are prepared to give some advice and they are giving splendid advice at the present time. But they realize, as do hon. members of this house and the country in general, that a great responsibility rests upon the members of parliament. They expect us to make proper provisions. They realize also that a responsibility rests upon the people of this dominion. I was surprised to hear one hon. member say this afternoon that the returned men are not looking particularly to industry for jobs.
The men in the armed forces hope that when this war is over there will be jobs for them. They know that the only way in which jobs can be provided is through industry. As the hon. member said, industry is for the production of goods, but goods cannot be produced without work. These men are hoping to obtain this work from industry. They believe that the government should see to it that they are given preference as far as work is concerned, not only by the government but by industry as well.
We who served in the last war remember how difficult it was for some to obtain positions after that war was over, but I believe that at least eighty per cent of the men who served in that war found employment when they came back. I do not think they were any burden upon this country. They did not want to be a burden. They were satisfied if they could obtain work through their own energy. I am sure that eighty or ninety per cent of the men in this war will come back and will rehabilitate themselves to as great an extent as did their fathers before them.
But there is always a minority which must be looked after. There are many men who give splendid accounts of themselves when they are fighting the enemy, but who do not seem to have the same success in fighting the battle of life. This country owes a great debt to those men and we must see that they suffer in no way. The question of pensions has been discussed fully in this house. A pension is not compensation, and I do not think the country or the government looks upon it as compensation to the men who have served in war.
I would ask this question of hon. members: How many of you would be willing to accept 850,000 for your right leg or right arm? How

Department of Veterans' Affairs
many hon. members would accept S100.000 for their eyes, or for the complete destruction of their nervous system? There is no price that would pay us for the destruction of our mentality. How many of us would accept any amount of money as compensation for the loss of a limb or any of our faculties? Therefore I say that a pension is not compensation to these men who have been wounded or disabled, because nothing compensates a man for the losses I have just mentioned. The men are hoping that if they have losses the pensions given them will provide a decent living, decent homes and decent opportunities for their wives and children. That is one of the things they feel should and must be provided for them.
Then, so far as the men themselves are concerned, they feel-and I say the country should feel-that they should be made as comfortable as possible under the circumstances in which they find themselves. Men returning wounded and maimed do not live normal lives. Most men like to join in certain activities such as sports, fishing, hunting, camping and so on. The wounded men are denied these privileges. For this reason we must, we should-and I know we do

take a very sympathetic attitude. We realize we owe a great debt.
The legislation which has been brought down in the house in. the twenty-five years following the last war. and during the four years of the present one, should be good. There is no question about that. I believe that if one were to compare the legislation in Canada providing for rehabilitation, pensions and the like, with similar legislation in other countries he would conclude that we have done very well in this country. If there has been any weakness-and I know there has been-it has been in the administration of that legislation. The men who have been acting in administrative capacities have not always approached their task with what might be described as a humane approach. Possibly they have carried out the letter of the law, but they have not always carried out its spirit. Nor have they carried out the intention of members of parliament- and I believe we are^all humane in this respect -or the intention of the public in general.
I should like to pay a tribute, if I may, to the Canadian Legion and to the other war organizations which have done so much for returned soldiers from 1919 until the beginning of this war, and during its progress. In those years the men in these organizations have picked out the flaws in whatever soldier legislation has been brought before the house. I know the Minister of Pensions and National

Health (Mr. Mackenzie) and other ministers have been helped immeasurably by the contribution these organizations have made.
Someone has said that men who were in the last war are getting old, and that the younger men who have taken part in the present war will have to take their places. That, of course, is a natural conclusion; but I know the men in this war will feel that the advice of many of the men who fought in the last one can be used to good advantage, and I am sure advantage will be taken of it.'
There have been difficult cases; we hear about them in the house. But of the hundreds of cases which are not difficult we hear very little. I am sure that only the difficult ones are brought to the minister's attention, and (hat he hears very little about the cases which have been worked out successfully under our legislation. This, again, to a great extent is due to the hard work performed by men in the Canadian Legion. I have had to handle many pension cases, but when I find a difficult one I usually send it to a representative of the Canadian legion, or to some other veterans' organization. I find they look after such cases much better than I can.
Another organization which comes under this legislation is the soldiers' land settlement board. Much has been said in this debate about the inequalities brought about by this board, and unfortunately, most of what has been said is true. The greatest attention should and must be given to settling men on the land. I think we might say, speaking generally, that the act passed at the time of the last war was not a success; there were many failures. Possibly there were reasons for those failures. No one could foresee what was going to happen. While failures occurred, still I am satisfied that those who tried to formulate the act did the best they could at the time.
After the last war I happened to be engaged for a few years in my own province as school inspector, and as such I had good opportunities to see how the act- was working. In many cases good land, buildings, stock and machinery were provided. But the price paid, was too high, and the men could not make a success. Another question which entered into the matter was the lack of farming experience of the men who were undertaking the work. Then, these men were also placed on farms in isolated districts.	They were away from
schools, telephones, churches and other social organizations. If we have learned from the experience of the past we shall see to it after this war every consideration is given to placing these men on farms where they will have

* Department of Veterans' Affairs
at least the social amenities and that they will have an opportunity of living normal lives.
Another mistake that was made was that, not only were the men inexperienced in farm life, but their wives were girls who had come from cities and towns. Many of them had come from the old country, and had not had experience either in working or in living on our Canadian farms. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) spoke about giving clear title to the men who are in debt on the farms. I believe that matter was also discussed by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). I agree wholeheartedly with what both these hon. members said.
Another matter upon which I should like to touch for a few minutes is the rehabilitation grant. I do not think that at the present time a sufficient grant is being given to the men who are discharged. A man is asked if he has a job, and if he says that he can go back to work he is given one month's rehabilitation grant, and is discharged from the army. I contend that no matter whether he was a carpenter, a farmer, a lawyer, a barber, a painter-no matter with what profession or craft he may have been connected-one month's rehabilitation allowance is not sufficient. Those men, upon returning, must enter into competition with others who have been doing that work for the three or four years the soldiers have been in the army. Their tools may be considerably worn, and they are not given enough money to buy new ones. If they turn to farming work they will have to purchase stock. Some of the men would have to stock farms which they had left three or four years ago and which have not since been cultivated. All these things would take more than one month's pay. In some cases two or three months' pay would be required, and in my view some provision should be made to give the men a larger grant than is permitted at present.
Yesterday the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) spoke eloquently about hospitalization. That is a subject he is well qualified to discuss. Apart from his criticism respecting some of the hospitals, it is within my knowledge that in Canada hospitals which have not been satisfactory have been used in the last twenty-five years. An hon. member spoke to-day of men going to hospitals and having to wait for doctors. I do not know whether, as the hon. member suggested, they were having afternoon tea or morning tea, but I agree with him that there has been a good deal of difficulty in this connection and that men have had to wait.
I suggest to the minister that these hospitals should be located in the finest surroundings it is possible to find. For men who are under hospitalization, the hospital is their home; it may be their home for years, and the very best conditions are none too good for them-not in some crowded urban area, but in a beautiful location, preferably where men can enjoy, in part, country surroundings and, in part, the amenities of city life.
I should like to know from the minister whether the care of war graves is provided for under this measure.

speechtext:
It seems to me that overseas graves might well have been included in a measure which relates to soldiers' affairs.
In past years in this chamber I have listened to considerable criticism concerning what has been done for returned soldiers and their dependents. We realize that not sufficient has been done in the past, but we also wonder whether hon. members or others who have criticized, during the past twenty-five years, the provision which has been made, could have done any better. The Pension Act and other measures on behalf of returned men have been in course of evolution; they have been tested and improved throughout all these years. I wonder whether twenty-five years ago those who are so critical to-day could have produced a perfect act. We know that the Pension Act has been amended time and time again; other acts in the interests of returned men have also been amended a great many times.
The treatment of soldiers after the great wars of recent times has been far from generous. As a matter of fact the veterans of Greek and Roman times were probably treated better than the fighting men of later days.
Department of Veterans' Affairs

Kipling points out that men are acclaimed as heroes during war time, but when the war is over, little attention is paid to them. After the Crimean war many soldiers were reduced to begging for a living. We know, too, the appalling conditions under which they lived during that great campaign. After the South African war, land grants were given to the volunteers who returned, but these men were exploited so far as their grants were concerned and very little money reached them from the sale of their lands. The great war was the first occasion when any real effort was made, at least by the parliament of this country, to see to it that the soldiers received justice and fair play. As I have said, a great many mistakes were made, but I believe that the people of this country and parliament representing the people made a real effort to deal justly with the veterans. As far as this war is concerned, there can be no excuse for this parliament or for the people of Canada if everything is not done that should be done with regard to the rehabilitation of returned men.
I ask the indulgence of the house to illustrate and emphasize the fact that in the past men who should have received great consideration were neglected. I have before me a copy of a soldiers' magazine, published in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, called On Parade, June, 1944, edition. It contains an article dealing with the first V.C. in British America. I wonder how many members of this house know that the first Victoria Cross awarded to a Canadian was won by a man of the name of Hall, the son of a slave. Hall was born in April, 1827, at Newport, Hants county, Nova Scotia. The article, which is written by Robert B. Blauveldt, describes how, in 1852, Hall became a Royal Marine on board His Majesty's Ship Rodney, on which he served throughout the Crimean war. In 1856 he joined the British ship Victory, and, after the outbreak of the Indian mutiny, he served in India, where General Sir John Inglis, also a native of Nova Scotia, was besieged in the Residency at Lucknow by an army of 50,000 sepoys. The garrison, reduced to a mere handful, were in desperate straits when help arrived. General Sir John Campbell, in charge of the relief force, decided to send from one of the ships a gun close under the walls in an effort to open a breach in the walls. The crew proved to be one man short, so that Hall, in charge of another gun, volunteered to fill his place. One after another the gun crew were killed under the murderous fire of the natives, until only two men, Hall and a Lieutenant Young, the latter badly wounded, remained to serve the gun. In the recital of the circumstances under which Hall won his V.C., it is said:

Finally, in one of the most supreme moments in all the age-long story of human courage, Hall fired the charge which opened the walls and enabled the British forces to push through to the relief of the garrison and, ultimately, to the quelling of the mutiny and the restoration of peace and order to India.
For this signal courage and devotion to duty Hall was recommended for and received the Victoria Cross.
In 1901, when the late King George V visited Halifax, Hall was honoured by being given a carriage in the procession, but soon afterwards he was forgotten. Three years later, in August, 1904, he died, and was buried in Hants county, Nova Scotia. The writer of the article goes on to say:
But to the everlasting shame of his native province-and, in fact, of the great empire which he had so nobly served-his mortal remains lie in an unmarked and neglected grave, under a tangle of bushes and briers, its exact location unknown except to the very few who have taken a personal interest in preserving the memory of one of an ungrateful country's greatest heroes.
I bring this to the attention of the house simply to show that we have come a long way as far as attention to our fighting men and recognition of our heroes are concerned. But I also bring this incident to the attention of the house in the hope that a great wrong, in the disregard of the memory of this brave man, will be righted. I hope that some historical society or some other organization in Canada will see to it that his memory receives fitting attention.
I think we should look to the future and not to the past as far as building up our institutions is concerned, so that our post-war world shall be built on a firm foundation. We must provide greater services, greater leisure, greater security, greater opportunity for our returned men and also for the people of our country.

speechtext:
I associate myself with hon. members who have spoken in favour of this bill to coordinate all the work pertaining to the veterans of this and the former war. Since the war began, more than 2,000 young men and women who passed through my classes in two schools in the years immediately preceding the war joined His Majesty's forces. As I listened to the news of the invasion last week I could not help thinking of the care-free life which those boys and girls lived, of their ambitions and their hopes, which they were forced to abandon on receiving a higher call to duty for their country. For their sake particularly, I am keenly interested in any legislation that will provide for their future welfare. I never see or hear from one of them without being asked what we at Ottawa are doing to prepare for their return to Canada. A great responsibility rests

Department of Veterans' Affairs
upon us here at this particular time. In n-o way can we show our gratitude for the work which they are carrying on at the present time better than by passing legislation that will grant them security after they return.
Two things are required of us: first, that we do everything humanly possible to contribute to their success during the war; second, that we do everything possible to make conditions in Canada worthy of the sacrifices they are making.
I should like to join with other hon. members in complimenting the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). In the light of the grand fighting speech which he made on behalf of our men in the forces, I am quite ready to overlook even his political gibes at this party. If the effect of his speech upon the members of the treasury board were anything like its effect upon the private members of the house, I would say he did a good day's work for his comrades.
I associate myself also with the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) in his fight for those veterans who secured land in western Canada after the last war, to obtain for them a clear title to that land. I had the privilege of meeting and talking with a deputation representing those veterans, and as I studied their brief, it appeared to me that the government would have been just about as far ahead if it had given those men free titles to the land to start with. The oost to the government has come very close to eating up all the income that the government has received from that project.
I think a good point from which to begin my speech would be to go back to a resolution adopted by the Liberal convention on August 7, 1919, a resolution on pensions moved by the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I think the house should recall that resolution:
That such pension or allowances be granted as shall enable the soldiers or their dependents as the case may be to maintain a liberal standard of living sufficient to guarantee health, education and all the necessities, comforts and amenities which go to make up a standard of living worthy of Canadian citizenship.
Incidentally, I may say that the word "liberal" in that resolution is spelt with a small and not a capital "1". That was on August 7, 1919. We have only to contrast with that resolution the facts regarding the treatment of men in the last war as borne out by history. I know of many scores of veterans of the last war to whom I would be ashamed to show that resolution to-day. What are the facts? Can we wonder that, as the hon. member for Vancouver North stated, the confidence of the people in promises of governments and
political parties is at a very low ebb at the present time. Governments since 1919-and this goes for both Liberal and Conservative governments-failed to provide adequately for the rehabilitation of able-bodied men who returned from the last war or to take ample care of those who came back incapacitated and disabled.
We talk about conditions under which no one who takes part in this war shall be worse off for his having done so. I wonder how many there were who took part in the last war who did not suffer by reason of the fact that they served their country. I need not dwell at length on the extent to which both governments failed to rehabilitate the men who returned, nor need I elaborate upon the extent to which both governments failed to provide adequately for those who were disabled. The fact is that vast numbers of men who fought in the last war are to this very day in need of the necessities of life. I know of instances in my own riding. I have taken some of those men to the chairman of the pension board, who was ready to admit that the men were entitled to more than they were getting, but said that there were cast-iron regulations which prevented him from doing for those men what he felt was the country's moral obligation.

there are men, scores of them, who have returned from this war who are this very day in need of the necessities of life, in need certainly of that which would give them a standard of living worthy of a Canadian citizen. I wonder how many of those regulations are actually made either by the minister or by his colleagues. I thought again during the years when I taught Canadian history that government was subject to the will of the majority of parliament. I have been forced to reach the conclusion that this is scarcely true; that regulatory bodies can make regulations and that these regulations can remain in force, although every member of the cabinet must know that the desire of the majority of the
Department of Veterans' Affairs

members of parliament are opposed to some of the regulations. I cited a couple of instances a few nights ago; I am going to refer to them again. I doubt if there is a private member who would support on the floor of this house the practice by which an old age pensioner's pension is reduced because his son overseas has assigned pay. I doubt if any private member in this house would support that principle; yet that practice, because it is a regulation, remains in force from day to day and many pensioners suffer thereby.
I wish to make a few general observations. We should realize once and for all that we cannot discharge our obligations to the men who are serving in this war by granting some cash pittances and then leaving them to fend for themselves. I think we all realize that at this time our obligations go much farther than that. To care for those disabled in the war and the rehabilitation of those who return able-bodied is, I believe we all recognize, the responsibility of the government. The cost of that care and rehabilitation must be considered as a part of the cost of the war. We shall not have paid for this war so long as an active participant in it or one of his dependents requires aid or rehabilitation; and just as we have been generous in providing all the material needs that it is physically possible for us to provide for the winning of the war, so we must be equally generous in providing for the human needs that arise out of the war. Just as we have never held up the production of anything material to the war on the excuse that there was no money for that job, so must we never permit one who has suffered because of participation in the war to go in want of any of the necessities of the life on the flimsy excuse that we as a nation cannot afford the expense. The country that can afford to spend $25,000, $35,000 or $40,000 for the training and equipping of young men for war can ill afford to let that man come back to civil life and go in need of anything that is essential to a standard of living worthy of Canadian citizenship.
Other hon. members have already referred to the word "pre-enlistment." I suggest that that word1 be deleted completely from the pension department's vocabulary. Thousands of veterans in this country to-day will recall their disappointment when on coming before the pension board they were informed they were non-pensionable because their physical disability was a pre-enlistment one. It is unfortunately true that men coming back from this war are still being deprived of pensions for the same reason. I have in mind one man in particular who was declared by the pension board to be non-pensionable because his dis-

ability was a pre-enlistment one. The man had a back ailment. I saw certificates, statements from former employers, showing that that man had been employed in firing a railway locomotive, working on a dock, working in a lumber yard, and they all bore evidence to the fact that in no case had he been unable to work because of any illness or weakness; yet his disability is declared to be pre-enlistment, I wish to join with those hon. members who have stated already that we should accept the principle that where a medical board has given a recruit the classification A-l, when that man comes before a pension board there should be no question of any pre-enlistment disability.
For a few moments I should like to deal with the training and educational programme of the government. I would suggest-I think there is need of this-that the department prepare a statement setting forth all the educational opportunities in every field, vocational and academic, to which a returned man or woman is entitled with government assistance. There may be such a record already, though I have been unable to find one. I am asked constantly by boys who are interested in improving their educational status whether this or that course is available to them and for how many years they may hope to get assistance in connection with their education. I believe that these educational opportunities should not be limited too rigidly, either because the young man or woman concerned did not give evidence of a desire to follow a particular course before enlistment, or because the length of service was not sufficient. Many of these boys have now spent four years away from Canada. Thousands of them left high school to enlist; others had not gone beyond public school. To-day who is to say what courses these young men would have followed in those four years if they had been permitted to live normal lives in normal times? We cannot give them back those four years which, from the point of view of gaining an education, are the most precious years of their lives. We can, however, give them every encouragement to make good that loss as far as that may be possible, and we should see to it that it is financially possible for them to do so. I urge that we should place no obstacle in the way of their getting whatever education they have the ability or the desire to obtain.
The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) made it quite evident that in his opinion no returned man should be required, either while undergoing training or until such time as he could get a job, to live on less than the pay and allowances he received while in the forces. This should be

Department of Veterans' Affairs
the case particularly in connection with all those up to army lieutenant or equivalent rank. I want to join with the hon. member in asserting that until the country is able to provide that man with a job, under no circumstances should he be required to live on less in peace time than we were willing to pay him in time of war.
I shall not delay the house by taking time to go into further detail. As other hon. members have said, very little research is required to discover that even the present S65 clothing allowance-which is so much better than the previous S35 allowance-is much too low to enable a returned man to secure a complete outfit of clothes at present prices. I am sure any investigation would show that anything less than $125 or $150 is inadequate. I should like to relate the rehabilitation programme to the entire reconstruction programme, but Your Honour ruled that discussion out of order when a previous speaker attempted to deal with it. Therefore I shall close with a couple of quotations, tire first from General Sir Archibald Wavell, spoken in Cairo on January 1, 1941:
Have you ever thought what a world we could make if we put into peace endeavours the same energy, the same self-sacrifice and cooperation as we use in the wastefulness of war?
The second quotation is by the VicePremier of Czechoslovakia, Jan Masaryk, as reported in the Saturday Evening Post of January 3, 1943:
Sooner or later we shall have to adjust ourselves spiritually and intellectually to the changes produced by this material revolution and reshape our institutions accordingly. In the field of economies the supremacy of the common good, as contrasted with selfish gains by a few, must be recognized and furthered by concerted national and international, private and public action.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my contribution to this debate which has to do with the setting up of a Department of Veterans' Affairs. I shall not detain the house at any length, because I am not going to repeat what has been said already during this debate by other speakers and in other words; what I wish to say is along perhaps somewhat different lines. I could never figure out why there should be any extended debate on the question of giving anyone security. I could never understand why there should be any argument to it, and this is particularly true in connection with those in our fighting forces who have offered their lives on the altar of sacrifice. Surely, if anyone in this country deserves security, it is these men who have offered their lives for their country. There should
be no argument about it. This sort of bill and subjects of this kind seem to involve a tremendous amount of debate. There can be only one reason for that. As far as 1 can see the government are not prepared to go as far as the members of this house think they should go in giving to these worthy men of our fighting forces the adequate security we think they shoidd have.
I have listened to hon. members who have preceded me and I was much taken with the speech yesterday of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). I could not help feeling that perhaps he should be with this group over here. He manifested some of the attitude toward monetary matters which this group has been recommending for a good many years. However, I think he was a little bit off in one or two things he said. For instance, he said that the policy of the government, his government, this government in power to-day, was that what is physically possible and desirable should be made financially possible. That never has been the policy of the Liberal party of this country.
We have been preaching that policy in this house for a good many years. As a matter of fact I think I can say without any fear of contradiction that that phrase was coined by none other than Major C. H. Douglas, one of the great world exponents of social credit and, I think I can say also without fear of contradiction, one of the greatest economic minds of the age. The hon. member for Vancouver North said that that was the policy of his government. If there was any semblance of truth in that, it has not been because this is the policy of the government; it is because the circumstances of the war have forced the government's hand to do financially what they were never able to do before. At least if they were able to do it, they refused to do it. The hon. member for Vancouver North also said that no financial obligation should stand in the way of the government giving our returned men that which is their due. I think we shall all agree with that. When the hon. member made that statement, by whom was he applauded? He was applauded by all the members on the opposition side. I noticed particularly that that statement was not applauded by members on the government side of the house.

Well, there were two. I am sure that is a glorious record. What was the statement? The hon. member for Vancouver North said that no financial obligation should stand in the way and I am told now that two Liberals applauded that statement. If there was ever a truer statement made than that I should like to know what it is. Applying that statement to this bill to establish a Department of Veterans' Affairs, I contend that if that department is established and is to be subjected to financial limitations, it will end where all other departments have ended, far short of the objective the people of this country want.
We know what happens under the present administration. We know that when a department desires to put over a programme-I am not complaining about its desires-it is subjected to the dictates of the treasury board. If the treasury board say, "We are sorry, we have no money," that ends it. It does not make any difference if the programme is physically possible or if it is desirable; if they say, "We have no money," that settles the question. I am wondering if a thing of that kind should be. As far as I am concerned, the whole thing is wrong. The fact of the matter is that the government should be able to do anything that is physically possible. Anything that parliament desires and moves that is physically possible, then the department or the government should say, "Very well; we are the servants of the people; you represent the people and we will do this; we will not let any financial limitation stand in our way."
One or two speakers have said that if this department is to be set up it must be provided with the proper machinery. I have no argument to offer there because I think that is so. But if that is all that is so, then it will fall far short of the mark. If it is administrators that we want I declare that you can get them in Canada for a dime a dozen. You can get the best administrators in the world. You can get the men who are at the head of industry, at the head of our financial institutions; if you like you can get the men who are at the head of our political movements. Put them all together; give them charge of this department, and if they do not have enough money they will fall down absolutely on the job.

I have not heard a great deal of criticism about the administrative ability of the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), and I have no criticism to offer of him as an administrator. However, I do not know that he is doing any better than any other cabinet material, either in the Liberal party or in any other party. We go to the Minister of Pensions and National Health and we say to him, "We notice that you are giving so much for clothing to our soldiers; we notice that you are giving them so much for allowance on demobilization; do you really think that is enough?"

However, I will not put words in his mouth. My next question would be, "Would you not like to give them more?" Of course he would say "yes." He has said he did not think it was enough. Then he would say, "Of course, I would like to give them more." "Well," we say, "why do you not?" What is the answer to be? There is only one answer, and that is, "Well, I am sorry, but the fellow higher up won't supply me with enough money."
The trouble is not in the administrative machinery. There may be a cog loose here, or a cog loose there, but I do not think the trouble is with the administrative machinery. The trouble is, always has been, and always will be under this or any old-line party administration, or any other administration subject to the present financial power, "Where are you to get the money?" That will be the trouble with any administration working under a debt economy.
There is not a great deal to offer when we talk about the kind of administration we should have. If my car stalls on the road I do not get out to see if the bumper is on wrong, or if the licence plate is hanging straight or if the windshield wiper is working. If the car stalls I want to find out what is fundamentally wrong. I want to see if the ignition works or if the gasoline is flowing properly. In examining legislation of this kind -and this applies to all post-war reconstruction, and matters of that kind-if there is

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
anything wrong with it when it is set up there is no use in going to this man or to that man or to the other man. Look for the fundamental error; and if the error is that there is not enough money, then let us admit that fact and either supply the money or put someone in power who knows where to get it.
I have just one further observation to make. I trust that people are not going to be fooled by this new department, or by the government's action in setting it up. There is a tendency to say, "Oh, this is a great thing; we are to have a new department of government, and it is to be known as the Department of Veterans' Affairs. That is a great thing; now we shall begin to go somewhere." I think I had better say that you are not going anywhere you have not been before. The setting up of a new department does not for one moment guarantee that our returned men will be cared for adequately. It is just another piece of machinery. The best way to show that the government means business is to start with the soldiers of the last war, many of whom are still in need, and with the soldiers who are now coming back from the present war. This does not need another department. Let us see that the government means business. When we see that the soldiers are treated better we shall know that the government means business. All the new departments in the world are not going to convince me or the legion or anybody else, unless they can show the people that this thing is being done.
I say, in closing, that it will not be done until the vital principle of the social credit philosophy, namely, that of making that which is physically possible and desirable financially possible, is accepted. Make the figures fit the facts.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to create a department which will be responsible for the care, treatment, training and reestablishment in social life of ex-members of the armed forces, and of persons otherwise engaged in pursuits relating to the war, and for the care of dependents of such persons. This is a laudable purpose, but it is entirely covered by the present act. The unfortunate thing is that the present act is not applied as it should be. There were legitimate grievances of the returned men and the men who have been discharged for one reason or another, and instead of those grievances being corrected we are told that a new department will be established. It is an old wagon with a new coat of paint, and with the old driver in the seat. There is practically no change, except that the matter has been studied very carefully by some zealous members.
But, sir, there is an easy way to correct these wrongs. To do so one has to come down to earth, come down from the clouds and try to improve the conditions of the returned men.
I regret having to repeat the same thing so many times. I have a soft thought for the minister, a congenial and likable man, much more so than some of his colleagues. In fact, he is so congenial that he could share that quality with them, and still keep enough to be well liked by all. How many times must I repeat that it is absurd not to give pensions to men who deserve them, or to men who have been promised pensions by the minister?
I hold in my hand data respecting regimental number D-554528, C. H. Pelletier, of Riviere-du-Loup. This man was riding a motorcycle in the bush for the first time, in process of doing some commando training. He was in company with a corporal. The motorcycle was then put on the road in high gear. The man in question sat on it, and as soon as he was in the saddle the corporal removed the clutch, with the result that the motorcycle went off at full speed and struck a tree. The man's leg was broken in three or four places, and he also suffered injuries to his spine. My understanding is that the leg was badly broken, and one or two inches of it were broken like dust. He went to the hospital, and his leg was in a plaster cast fur several months. Then I had the promise of the department that he would have a pension in August- He went several times to Quebec. He can hardly walk; his wife asked for a pass, but it was refused. Finally, upon my advice, he reported to the doctor, came back, and got nothing. He repeated this several times. It is evident that this man was badly hurt while in the service through the guilty carelessness and criminal negligence of a non-commissioned officer, and is entitled to a pension. I have the promise of the minister, who writes me very fine letters about the matter, but nothing comes from the pension department for this man. It is a sad case. When I meet him I give him something. Although my means are limited I try to help him, but what I can give him is negligible. The other day he came to my office and asked me to write a letter to his bank manager to say that I am working to obtain him a pension. "Tell him," he said to me, "that you are trying to get me a pension. I owe him $25 but I cannot pay it. My wife works a little; I cannot work at all. I hope that, with a letter from you, the bank manager will grant a renewal of my note."
At a time when we hear so much about what is to be done for the veterans, why not begin now? There must be a start. When will the start be? Will it be made only after
Department of Veterans' Affairs

the war is over? That is absurd. A beginning should be made now. There is no excuse for the pensions branch not paying a pension to that man. To-day is June 15; I was told by the minister in August last that the man would have a pension; but the board are so stubborn and their attitude is so unbelievably absurd that, as recently as last Monday, when I met this man on the street, walking with difficulty, and asked if he had got anything, he said, "no." One reproach which was made [DOT] against him was that he did not go to the hospital when the doctor told him to. But he had been there for months. He had a conversation with a doctor in Quebec city who, having told him that it was useless for him to take hospital treatment, afterwards told him that he should go there. So that soldier said, "If it is useless for me to go there, why should I go?" He needs the means wherewith to live, but so far he has got nothing.
Here is another case, of E-621922. I have a big file here dealing with this case, which is that of a man named Yvon Belanger. He had pleurisy in one lung. While he was in the army he contracted pleurisy in the other lung, imputable to his service, since it occurred while he was in the service. He was told to resign from the army, and that he would have an opportunity to go home right away. This is the policy of some doctors, especially of the pensions branch.

In spite of what my hon.
friend has said, that case has a bearing on the discussion, for this reason. It is my view that when a man is put in category "A", when he is admitted into the army and is afterwards put in a lower category, it means that he has contracted some disability in the army, and it is most important that that examination should be made with care. In my humble view, a man who is in good health when he goes into the army, and who is not so well, or is disabled, when he is discharged has a right to be compensated by the government for that.
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

There was the case of another man who suffered from lung trouble. He contracted a cold that was not well looked after. He received no pension. His number is E-621251. There was also the case of Alfred Levesque, No. 23203. He is a veteran of the last war. I shall send this file to the minister. Parts of it are in French. I have letters from the parish priest. I have no secret to keep from anybody. This is an open book. I prefer to handle the matter in this way in order to put the least possible on the record. I still expect that some improvements will be made.
Then I have the case of Moise Robillard, C-10542. He was at Christie street hospital. He has been discharged. He has had very little. There is a connection between the medical examination in the army and the right of a soldier to a pension. Then I received a letter from the Canadian AntiVivisection Society, Victoria, British Columbia, with regard to the case of a man named Reuben W. Carlier, who died at Neepawa, Manitoba, after an injection of toxoid. He was a British airman. These cases come from all over. I am sending a copy of this letter to a doctor who complained that I was too hard on the medical faculty. I hope that the minister will take up these cases and will see to it that the thing is corrected so as to give the soldiers some faith in the future, and so that they will not lose confidence. At the present time such treatment has a very bad effect. All those men who are not treated as they should be have relatives and friends. This is all known to them. It has a very bad effect on recruiting and on the morale not only of the unit, but on the people who are at home, the relatives of those men.
What about other cases? There was a man who was totally deaf. He was put in category "A" in Quebec on September 12, 1939. He was put in category "E" at Sussex, New Brunswick. He was again placed in category "A" on June 6, 1941, and in category "E", five pulhems at Dartmouth in December 1943. When he was examined in Quebec city he was O.K. But when he was examined more carefully at other places such as Dartmouth and Sussex on two occasions he was placed in category "E". Those are many things that require correction and I hope that it will be done at once.
The minister has the power to instruct the officials of his department to do their duty properly to the men in the service, and to notify his officials that if they do not do so, if they do not act in accordance with the letter and the spirit of the law, he will fire them.
I do not want the death of the sinner; I want

his conversion. It is the last time that I shall say that with regard to the department
of pensions.
The men in my county have been treated very badly. When I spoke to some hon. members from Ontario they said that they were satisfied with the treatment the men had received here. How is it that it is only in the province of Quebec that the men do not get the treatment they have a right to expect from the pension board? There are reforms to be brought about in the army and in the department of pensions, as well as in many other places. Reforms in the department of pensions are the most urgent and I trust that the minister will see to it that those men are better treated.
Before concluding my remarks I wish to refer to another case which seems to be unusual. There was a big man that I have known, and unfortunately I have already mentioned this case without any success. His number is E-100257. He was a very strong and powerful man. He was on guard in Quebec city. He was given shoes that were too small for his feet. He could not wear other shoes. He asked for some but did not get them. He had to wear the regulation Shoes. He tried to wear them for some time, and they hurt his feet so badly that he can hardly walk and sometimes he cannot work for two or three weeks in a month. This is cruel and inhuman. What did that man have? It was true that he suffered very much; it was true that this came on during his service. His disability was assessed at five per cent for bronchitis and five per cent for a scar on his right foot. However, the commission ruled that the bronchitis was of pre-enlistment origin, not aggravated during service and that, therefore, no pension was payable in respect of it. The pension was paid at five per cent, effective from the day of his discharge in respect of the disability from the scar on his right foot. The letter from the commission reads:
As you, of course, know the assessment of disability is on direction of the medical advisers of the commission. In Mr. Cloutier's case we consider the award of pension in accordance with his degree of disability. I regret I cannot give you a favourable reply.
That is unfortunate. It is not true. Imagine what this poor fellow who enlisted voluntarily had to suffer! He -was there on guard voluntarily. He had a right to have shoes that were fit for his feet. He asked for the shoes. Evidently they had some, but he could not get any. He could not buy regulation shoes anywhere. He did not want to steal any. He made an effort to remain on guard wearing shoes that were too small. He thereby injured his feet, which is acknowledged by the com-

Department of Veterans' Affairs
mission. Finally he received a small amount as a pension, although at times he cannot *work for two or three weeks in a month because his feet swell and he cannot wear any shoes. The minister is a kind-hearted giant-
I say that very seriously. I hope that he will be moved by these facts which deserve full consideration. Those men are well known to me. I have tried to help them, and I am getting tired of repeating the same things over and over again. However, I do it for a good cause and in the hope that these wrongs will be redressed in the near future.
