speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the success or failure of the Department of Veterans' Affairs has depended in the past and will depend in future on the understanding of the problem which such a department is designed to meet. We cannot hope to accomplish very much if we attempt to legislate for personal and individual cases. Perhaps in connection with no subject commonly discussed in this house is it easier to dramatize the discussion, because whoever speaks has lying ready to his hand all the elements of tragedy, and we must always guard against drifting into emotional fields. But we have twenty-five years of experience to guide us and, as a result of that experience, a classification of the problem, an understanding of which I think is essential if any discussion with respect to veterans' problems is to be helpful.
The indisputable fact is that from the outset it is essential to separate veterans' affairs into two divisions. The first division is that Concerning responsibility for those members of the services who have suffered disability in mind or body and who are or in the course of time will become pensioners. The record of Canada with respect to veterans disabled in the last war has been good. It is not good enough to say, as one hon. member said the other afternoon, that it is good only in comparison with previous experiences, which were exceedingly bad. The treatment of pensioners in Canada, with those unfortunate and inglorious exceptions with which we are all familiar, has been better than the treatment afforded to disabled veterans by any of our allies in the last war, and represents a type of world leadership of which we can be very proud. The second division includes all those who were on active service in any of the services. Following the last war that was a particularly vexed problem, because we had no experience. Even at that we produced the veterans' allowance board, which I submit was the most advanced legislation in the world dealing with the responsibility of government for those who had not suffered disabilities which could be established and pensioned.
Not only did we lack experience in the period following the last war; but those veterans who had not suffered noticeable and easily detected disabilities began to fail in their attempt to provide for themselves, just about the time this country entered the greatest economic depression which Canada and, in fact, the world had ever seen. Throughout that period we had discussion as to where the responsibility lay for those veterans who were not pensionable but who were destitute. In the beginning the responsibility was held to be local. As the problem became progressively greater, the responsibility became provincial and eventually, when it reached its full magnitude, there came a realization that the primary responsibility lay with the federal authority. All through that discussion, which dealt with the problem of destitution generally, it was argued-and with that argument I agree-that the responsibility for those who had been on active service was indeed federal, since the soldiers of Canada did not fight for a province but fought for the dominion.
This principle of governmental responsibility having been accepted as to the first division, relating to pensions, it seems unreasonable that the same general principle should not apply in the second division, dealing with all those who were on active service. By the same token, then, the loss of seniority in a job, the loss of a skill, the sacrifice of productive years and the invisible wounds of the spirit, though they be not pensionable, are indeed the responsibility of the national government. In a desire to spur successive governments following the last war, and particularly in recent times, to avoid the errors which occurred then and the failures; we have had expressed in this house great concern and fear for the future, fears which to my mind are not warranted by the record of the past. As a result we have induced in the minds of many of our people who are serving, and many of our people at home, a degree of trepidation which is not warranted by the history of our legislation. Approximately 600,000 Canadians served in the last war, of whom about 225,000 were Canadian born. The remainder fought as Canadians and brought imperishable honour to Canada as Canadians. Those who survived returned to Canada, and the history of how they became absorbed into the life of this country is not such as to warrant the oft-repeated criticisms of that post-war period. When we consider what the veterans of this war will return to I think it is worth while to study for a moment or two the conditions to which those who came back from the last war returned. Thousands of them had been less than five years in Canada. They had no homes, no jobs, and many of them had but
Department of Veterans' Affairs

very few friends. In my own experience I know of a little town where, of the first eleven men who enlisted, ten were not Canadian born. They had no homes and, in reality, no stake in the community. Seven of them returned, all of whom after a little time, with no other inducement than their own determination to be independent and to have a stake in the country of their adoption, succeeded in reestablishing themselves. All in all, in spite of 'the conditions that existed, we did not do badly.
The situation which will greet our returning soldiers this time is vastly different. More than ninety per cent of those in the services to-day were born in Canada and will return to their own homes. I have said that those who returned from the last war did not do badly. The proof of that statement is to be found in every community, in the long list of veterans of that war who are now the leaders, the backbone of business, of church and of state. It is to be found in the record of their children, their sons and daughters who serve in every branch of Canada's war effort to-day. I know there were those who fell short of the achievements I have mentioned, some through their own fault. Some were exploited commercially, some were exploited politically, some were caused to suffer by bad legislation, and more perhaps by the poor interpretation and administration of good legislation. Wellmeaning people who might have helped to alleviate the situation were cowed by the depression and the period of economic scarcity, and much less was done than we think could have been done under those conditions. But the conditions which prevailed in those depression years were more than a veteran problem.
The shadow of those years still darkens the hearts of parents and it dulls the hopes of youth in the service. I am sure it haunts the minds of honest employers who turn their attention to these problems in industry and consider what is to come again. The other day the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) suggested a policy and practice by which any veteran would be allowed to train on the same economic level as that on which he was trained for war. I venture to say that that suggestion is unanswerable; yet before we concur in it in its entirety there are questions to be answered, and I should like to propose some of those questions to-night.
How and by whom is the veterans' aptitude for training to be measured? We must remember that in the service he was trained for a specific job. Will his training be geared to his own desire or to his measured aptitude 
for the task? Will he be obliged to commit himself as to where he plans to use his newly acquired or retrained skill? Will his choice be governed by information made available by adequate surveys of the opportunities in his chosen locality? If it is to be a question of, "What would you like to do and what would you like to train for; here is a living while you train," how will the job balance be maintained not only in the community in which he lives but throughout Canada as a whole?
Something is being done with respect to this problem. To-day the soldiers returning to the various depots to be discharged from the Canadian services are interviewed first by the army examiners with whom they became familiar in the service. Part of the document known as WD-12 is prepared in conjunction with the officers of the Department of Pensions and National Health. This is a positive document which records the man's achievements in the service. It fills in the gap mentioned the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver North when he was referring to Lever Brothers, and their problem of getting information about the man's service. I am glad to say that this particular document is available in most districts to those officers of selective service whose duty it is to classify these returned veterans for positions in civil life in their community.
I should like to think and I would hope that that information, the appraisal part of that document, will be part of the record of the soldier which goes into selective service in the district to which he desires to go. Better still, I should like to see discharged veterans, both male and female, carry with them a record of the skills they have acquired, the training they have had and the advancement they have undergone during the period of their active service.
Not so long ago the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) stated that the returning personnel from the services did not want to be pampered. He might have added that they are not going to be fooled by demagogues who dishonour them by bidding for their support. Fortunately, between the two wars we in Canada have been singularly free from that kind of political jobbery with respect to veterans. It is my hope-and I see some indication that this hope may be realized- that this condition will continue in Canada and that we shall not have that type of bidding which dishonours but does not fool the people at whom it is directed.
Before we go into the second division dealing with the responsibilities of governments to the returning personnel who come back with-

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
out having suffered actual disability-' or damage in body or mind, we should perhaps make some estimate of the service they have performed. It is idle to say that everyone who volunteered did so with the idea of giving his life for his country. The man who volunteered no doubt realized that he might be called upon to make the supreme sacrifice for his country and he expressed the courageous willingness to do so, but that is not the only thing that motivated the men who enlisted. They went active for a variety of reasons. Sometimes there was a patriotic urge to do something about the despoiler of civilization; sometimes they did so through sheer boredom ; sometimes it was hunger; sometimes there were other personal reasons. I once interviewed a man who was doing his one thousand, one hundred and seventy-first day of detention over a period of three years. Rather abruptly I asked him, "Why on earth did you join the army?" He said, "Frankly, to get away from my wife."
That was an exceptional case, but I think it illustrates the danger we may get into if we consider this problem from the purely sentimental point of view of enlistment. There is a debt upon us to every one who volunteered for active service, no matter from what impulse, a debt which can never be repaid. Consequently it is more important that we should concern ourselves with those debts which can be repaid rather than to try to assess one man's or one woman's service as against another's with lesser service or in a different theatre of war. I should regret to see anything get into our legislation which would tend to create that discrimination.
This question of the obligation of the state to those who perform the highest duties of citizenship involves more than that. It has been raised already in this house. It involves some attempt to fix the differential between those citizens who do their duty in active service and those w-ho do their duty in any other capacity for which they were capable and to which they were physically limited. I think it is hopeless to try to do that by legislation. This is one place where we must trust administration to attempt to draw the line between common sense and sentiment.
This department which is being set up-it is really not a new department-must cooperate in a large way with local committees and local employers. I think this can be illustrated by giving the details of a case. A boy- at the age of nineteen was making $90 a month as a valued employee of a large concern. To-day he is a lieutenant in the army; he has reached the age of twenty-four, is married and has one child. He leaves the service and desires to
go back to the firm where he worked previously'. However, he has no skill or training which would make him valuable in any better capacity' than the $90 a month job he had before.
This department, in conjunction with the employer, or, where there is no employer, in conjunction with selective service, should devise some system of part work and part training. I know that is being done. With that cooperation a chap of this kind could work while training himself for a job which would be suitable to his capabilities and which would support himself and his family in adequate fashion. For such procedure I, for one, would hold up both hands for the suggestion of -the hon. member for Vancouver North. In the case of planned training for a specific job there can be no reason and no excuse for paydng less to the man in training for that job than he received when he was being trained for a specific job in active service. Unless this training is tied up to a specific job-opportunity, or at least based on established knowledge as the result of known opportunities in the locality in which he elects to live, then I am apprehensive that few more than the two or three per cent who at present take advantage of training will really be willing to take the training.
I think we talk too much in general terms when we speak of change, training and adjustment. We speak as though only by some upheaval of the conditions in which these men lived before they served could we hope to accomplish anything, or could any good come. I am inclined to think that if as many Canadians were looking boldly forward to-night as there are looking fearfully behind, this shadow of fear for the future of rehabilitation and reestablishment would pass from us. And, if by being fearful we inculcate fear in the minds of our returned youth in Canada we are doing them a great disservice.
If we train our returning youth to grasp security with both hands we shall never reach, or rise to the heights which some of us, at least, may have visualized for the future of Canada. Let us then care first for those who have suffered damage, and enable them to establish themselves in a way that they may not suffer as a result of that disabling incapacity. Having assured this, then perhaps if we fight and work for a new Canada which will give new opportunities as well as security7, and, if we meet to-day's problems in an adequate and satisfactory manner such as will give, hope and confidence to those who are returning, those who will return and those who wait for others to return, we shall have undertaken for the moment the main duty and
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

the greatest opportunity of the newly-reconstituted department. At a later time, when we are in committee on the bill, I shall have something further to say with respect to some of the problems which arise because of the difference between the conditions in the last war and those in this one.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT TO DEAL WITH THE CARE, TREATMENT, TRAINING OR REESTABLISHMENT OF MEMBERS OF THE ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is described as an act to establish a Department of Veterans' Affairs. My understanding of the work of this new department is that it is to be responsible for all matters concerning war veterans. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made that very clear when he moved the resolution preceding the bill. These were his words, as they are reported at page 2102 of Hansard:
Parliament is anxious to make the fullest provision for all matters that are likely to arise which may have a bearing upon their interests-
That is the interests of the veterans.

through the period that is to follow at the conclusion of this terrible war.
Then the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) used words to the same effect, and in the same debate, as follows:
. . . the idea being that all measures affecting generally the welfare and rehabilitation into civil life of the members of our forces will be embraced within the ambit of the measure which will follow upon the resolution which is now before the committee.
So that I propose this evening to review this bill, having in mind that question, as to whether or not it is broad enough to enable the new department to deal with all matters of concern to war veterans.
I believe the house is unanimous in wishing to make the bill broad enough and modern enough and realistic enough to accomplish that purpose. This is one of those occasions, which are not so rare as the public believe, when all members of the house are trying to do a good job, and are cooperating to see that this bill is the best possible measure that can be enacted by the parliament of Canada.
Looking at the bill, and having in mind the test as to whether or not it meets the problem, I find several weaknesses which I consider fundamental. I believe they are serious weaknesses, and I urge upon the minister and the house that amendments be brought in to strengthen these weak spots in the bill. The first weakness, to my mind, is that the bill seems to have the approach of the last war. It reads as though it had been drawn by men who fought in that war. I am one of those men myself, and I think there is a grave danger that those of us who served in the last war are apt to judge everything by what hap-

pened to us. The fact is that conditions in the present war are vastly different, and there is need of a new approach.
I say that this bill has been drawn, having in mind the wai of 1914-18. If members go through it carefully they will find that it closely resembles the Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment Act, which is chapter 187 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. That was a measure which set up the first department to deal with soldiers after the last war. Furthermore, this bill is almost identical with part I of the Department of Pensions and National Health Act, passed in 1928 as chapter 39 of the statutes of that year.
Then, the duties, powers and functions given this new department under the bill are not wide enough. They are set out in section 5, the opening words of which are these:
The duties, powers and functions of the minister shall extend and apply to the administration of statutes enacted by the parliament of Canada, and of orders of the governor in council, as are not by law assigned to any other department of the government of Canada or any minister thereof-
And these are the key words:
-relating to the care, treatment, training, or reestablishment in civil life. . . .
Those are the key words. They do not go far enough. I say that the section should cover such things as rehousing the men in the present war. That is a very serious problem, and one which presents one of the greatest difficulties for the men returning from the war, particularly those w'ho are married. As we know, many thousands of Canadian sailors,: soldiers and airmen have married overseas. I have here a clipping from the Vancouver Province of June 7-about a week ago; it is headed, "Soldier Looks for House", and then, in quotation marks, "Sorry I Ever Came Back". The article goes on to say:
"I'm sorry I ever came back to Canada," is a familiar lament at the national housing registry these days, say officials here as 63 discharged servicemen and their families look for a place to live.
Most of the men have seen service on the battlefield. One was a prisoner in a Japanese prison camp.
The article then refers to one discharged man who belonged to our famous Seaforth Highlanders of Canada and who had been disabled overseas. He came back with his wife and three-year-old daughter, had been in Vancouver since May, and, the article states:
. . . since then they have been living in damp housekeeping rooms or separate boarding houses.
"We were happy in England," he said. "We had a little cottage in Surrey, with a garden, and chickens and rabbits."

Department of Veterans' Affairs
A card telling about post-war rehabilitation plans was given to him on discharge. "But how do we get them?" he said.
He is only one of the hundreds who are having the same difficulty.
Therefore, I say, Mr. Speaker, that power should be given to the new department under section 5 of the bill to deal with the re-housing of soldiers. It will never be adequately dealt with by any other department.
Another matter is that of the repatriation of the dependents of our men from Great Britain. This will be one of the great problems affecting veterans of the present war. Already men are being sent back and discharged as unfit; yet their wives and children cannot cross the sea to their new homes in Canada. That, too, should be handled by this Department of Veterans' Affairs. It will never be adequately handled if it is the responsibility of any other department, because with another department the operation would be only a side-show, and if it did not get the last consideration it would be very close to the last.

speechtext:
The repatriation of the dependents of our men in the forces should be under this Department of Veterans' Affairs rather than one or other of the defence services, or the Department of Mines and Resources, where it is now-the immigration branch.
As to gratuities, the speech from the throne this year stated that during the present session a measure was to be brought down to provide war service gratuities. The session is drawing to a close; yet that legislation has not been introduced. Each day is important, because each day men are being discharged in Canada, and discharged without an adequate gratuity, with the result that they are handicapped just that much in settling back into civilian life. I suggest that these war sendee gratuities should also be handled by the Department of Veterans' Affairs, and that power so to handle them should be set out in the present bill.
I come to the question of employment. There is nothing in section 5 which gives the department power to deal with the matter of employing veterans. It is true that power is given to deal with their reestablishment, but that is only the beginning. A man may be
reestablished when he comes back, and then in a year or two he may be faced with unemployment. Those of us who were in the last parliament know what a terrible problem that was in the years from 1935 to 1940; and as the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) has said, most of us became convinced that the care of these men was the responsibility of the dominion government. Sooner or later th? question of who is to be responsible for finding work for unemployed veterans will come up again; and I suggest that power to meet that difficulty should be conferred in this bill upon the Department of Veterans' Affairs.
Also there should be power under section 5 to advise veterans. That is not set out here. At the present time there is no adequate provision for advising them either as to their rights and privileges or as to their opportunities. I know there are government officers whose duty it is to find out what jobs men are most likely to be suited to, but we must go farther than that. This department should be responsible for advising the men as to the occupations which are most likely to be open; and that, of course, would mean close collaboration by the various departments of government-munitions and supply, which would have to give some idea as to what types of manufacturing are to be carried on after the war, and other government departments. At the present time, I understand, these men get no idea of what types of jobs are likely to be available; they are simply asked what they would like to be and then, perhaps, given training for that particular calling. But we must go very much farther, and must advise them where there are most likely to be jobs.
Strangely enough, the one change made in section 5 is to delete from that section the power to care for the dependents of these men of ours who are coming back from the forces. In the Pensions and National Health Act of 1928 the last words of section 5 were, " and to the care of the dependents of such persons." [DOT] I can only believe that these words were left out of this section by an oversight. Certainly that power should be given to the new department. Allusion to the care of dependents does appear in several other sections of the bill, but not in this key section 5.
Strangely, too, there is no mention in section 5 of pensions-no power given to the department to deal with pensions. That was not in either of the other acts to which I have referred. I do not suppose it is material, because the department will have to deal with pensions, anyway, but I suggest that words giving the power to deal with pensions should be inserted in section 5. If that change is made, perhaps the minister would consider using, instead of the word " pension," the

words " war disability compensation," or words to the like effect. The use of the word "pension" may convey to some people the notion that the recipient is getting something for nothing, whereas if the words "war disability compensation" were used, one is reminded of the workmen's compensation, and it gives an entirely different idea

speechtext:
So much for suggestions with regard to the powers of this department. I think they can be made adequate only by an amendment of section 5 of the bill.
Then I suggest that in the bill provision should be made for the honorary committees which have already been appointed across Canada to assist in the rehabilitation of the men coming back from the war. I believe that these committees are doing good work. They are serving on an honorary basis, and I know that in my home city of Vancouver these men are trying very hard to help in the reestablishment of the soldiers who are coming back. But there is no mention of such committees in the bill, and I would point out that in the Veterans' Assistance Commission Act, which is chapter 47 of the statutes of 1936, provision was made for these honorary committees. The minister will find it in section 7 under the heading, "Honorary Local Committees". It provided that the veterans' assistance commission-
. . . with the approval of the minister, may appoint honorary local committees, composed of persons resident in any locality willing-
. (a) to assist the commission in obtaining information relating to veterans which may be required for classification of unemployed veterans.
This act, by the way, was passed when we were faced with the need of finding employment for many thousands of veterans of the last war.
(b)	to investigate and report to the commission upon measures and means in respect to the employment of veterans;
(c)	to assist the commission in enlisting the cooperation of employers' and employees' associations as well as of such other public and private agencies as may be in a position to provide employment for veterans;
(d)	to aid the commission in any other way in carrying out the provisions of this act.
[Mr. Green 1
We already have honorary committees established to aid in rehabilitation, and I suggest that they should be given statutory recognition.
Provision should also be made in the bill giving the minister and the new department authority to cooperate with other governmental bodies and agencies. Similar power was given to the veterans' assistance commission. The minister will find that in section 9 they were given the job of investigating and reporting to the minister upon-
. . . ways and means of cooperation between the commission and
(a)	any other commission or department of the government,
(b)	any provincial government or agency thereof,
(c)	any veterans' association,
(d)	any commercial, agricultural or industrial group or organization.
The act went on to say that it was the duty of the commission to cooperate with these various other bodies. I am confident that if some such provision is inserted in this bill it will make it all the easier for us to get results. The Department of Veterans' Affairs will certainly have to cooperate very closely with such other dominion departments as national defence, munitions and supply, and labour, and, I think, also with the provincial governments and the veterans' associations, and with commercial, agricultural and industrial groups across Canada.
These suggestions I submit for the purpose of meeting the first great weakness in this bill, and I hope that the minister will see fit to adopt at least some of them before the bill becomes law. The second weakness in the bill is this, that the new department is not limited to veterans' affairs. I think it should be limited to looking after matters that concern war veterans. Goodness knows, these matters are going to be numerous and difficult enough without giving this new department . any other job to do. When I refer to veterans, I include men of the merchant navy. I heartily agree with the statement made to-day by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) about the merchant navy being treated as a fourth arm of the service. They are so considered by His Majesty the King, and all of us feel that they are in the war just in the same way as the navy, the army and the air force.

Yes; that is correct. We would have lost the war without them. I am of the opinion also that such men as those in the auxiliary services and the Canadian

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
corps of fire-fighters should be given similar treatment; all those men who are really serving with the forces should be included in the bill. They should be _treated in the 6ame way as the men in the forces. I was very much struck by a letter received from one man in the auxiliary services actually serving with the troops in Italy. He came back from a tour of the line to find a notification in regard to his income tax. All the men in the forces overseas are free from income tax, but these other men in the merchant navy, the auxiliary services and the corps of fire-fighters are not. This is the letter this man wrote:
The information in regard to payment of income tax was conveyed to me in December, 1943, while serving on the battlefront. It was imparted to me at a most grotesque time, when I had just returned from a point where the fighting was desperate, where the dead were lying by the side of the road and in the streets of a certain town and everything was foul and there was a terrible stench everywhere. I came back and was told that because I was only a camp follower I had to pay income tax. It might be a good idea to ask whoever was responsible for the issue of the decree to come out with me and share my work for a month or two.
These men of the legion, the Y.M.C.A., the Knights of Columbus, the Salvation Army are with the Canadian troops in France to-night, and yet they have to pay income tax. That is not right. These men, and the other groups to whom I have referred, should be treated as the men of the forces are. But this bill goes farther. Hon. members will find in the explanatory note the following words:
The purpose of this bill is to establish a Department of Veterans' Affairs under the direction of a Minister of Veterans' Affairs who shall be responsible for the care, treatment, training, or reestablishment in civil life of ex-members of the armed forces and of persons otherwise engaged in pursuits relating to the war, and for the care of the dependents of such persons.
In section 5 we find the words "of any person" after the words I have quoted previously in my remarks. The similar section in the Department of Pensions and National Health Act referred to men who had served in the forces. This goes farther and refers to "any person". And by the tvay, the section might be considered broad enough to make the new department responsible for all vocational training of civilians, soldiers and anybody else. It could be construed in that way.

The third serious weakness in this bill is this paragraph (g) of subsection 1 of section 7, which I have read. It, too, is entirely new. It provides for pensions by regulation of the minister approved by the governor in council. That is a dangerous provision. Any right to pension should be statutory. It should not depend on any order in council or the whim of _ any minister. Furthermore, it may go so far as to enable the minister or the department to give a pension to favourites or to people who should not be entitled to them at all. I cannot understand why the government brings down a bill which contains this entirely new principle. I submit it is a very dangerous one. As the bill now reads, this provision is another blow at the merit system in the civil service of Canada, a blow in the case of a new and important department which will have many employees, which will face frightfully difficult problems, a department which we hope will be staffed by young Canadians, men of high ideals, men who are willing to sacrifice, their lives for the country.
In connection with this fourth weakness in the bill may I suggest to the minister, as several other members have suggested this afternoon, that young men of the present war should be appointed to responsible posts in the new department. I think they should be given some of the executive posts, and some of them should be made members of the Canadian pension commission. Perhaps we old soldiers are good enough to deal with the problems of the men of the last war, but I think something more will have to be provided to meet the problems of the men of the present war. I strongly recommend to the minister that he see to it that many of these young men are included in the staff of the new department. Provision has been made by the civil service commission for the calling for applications from men overseas for government appointments. I think they should be used particularly in the case of this department.
Those are the weaknesses that I see in the bill and the suggestions that I have to remedy them. In closing, I would point out to hon. members that the re-settling of our men from the forces is a very broad and difficult problem. The possibilities for good or ill to Canada in

connection with the work of this department are almost boundless. I believe that one of our main responsibilities as a parliament is to see to it that these young men get a proper start upon their return to civil life. I believe, further, that the future of this nation will shortly be in the hands of these young men and women from our forces.
